title: respectful action
explain: Put -(으)시- inside a word to show respect for the person doing the action, like a teacher or elder: 들어오셨어요 = (they) came in.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -시- after a vowel (가시다), -으시- after a consonant (읽으시다). It comes before tense markers and endings (가셨어요, 가시겠어요).

examples.en: The teacher came into the classroom.
My father reads the newspaper.

note: Use it only for the subject being honored, never for yourself; do not add it to 있다 (use 계시다) or to 먹다 (use 드시다).

title: formal polite statement
explain: Put -ㅂ니다/습니다 at the end of an action or description to speak in a formal, respectful way: 갑니다 = I go.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -ㅂ니다 after a vowel (갑니다), -습니다 after a consonant (먹습니다). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 삽니다).

examples.en: I am a student.
I get up at seven every morning.

note: Formal and polite; used in presentations, news, the military and with customers, not in casual talk.

title: everyday polite ending
explain: Put -아요/어요 at the end of an action or description for friendly, polite daily speech: 마셔요 = I drink.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -아요 if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (좋아요), otherwise -어요 (먹어요). 하다 becomes 해요, and many stems contract (가다 → 가요, 마시다 → 마셔요).

examples.en: I drink coffee every day.
The weather is really nice.

note: The same form works as a statement, question, suggestion or command; intonation and context tell them apart.

title: past action
explain: Put -았/었- inside a word to say something already happened: 만났어요 = met.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -았- if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise -었- (먹었어요). 하다 becomes 했-, and 이다 becomes 이었-/였-.

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
It rained a lot last week.

note: Irregular stems change before it (듣다 → 들었어요, 덥다 → 더웠어요).

title: it is (everyday polite)
explain: Add N이에요/예요 after a word to say 'it is that' in friendly polite speech: 책이에요 = it's a book.
attaches: Noun + 이에요 after a consonant (학생이에요), 예요 after a vowel (의사예요). Negative uses N이/가 아니에요.

examples.en: This is my book.
I am a doctor.

note: The copula is pronounced 이에요/예요, not 이어요; after a vowel the 이 contracts to 예요.

title: is doing
explain: Use -고 있다 to say an action is happening right now: 읽고 있어요 = I'm reading.
attaches: Verb stem + -고 있다, with no change after a vowel or a consonant.

examples.en: I am reading a book now.
My younger sibling is sleeping in the room.

note: With verbs like 입다 and 쓰다 it can mean a continuing state ('is wearing'). The honorific is -고 계시다.

meaning: nominalizer: the act of doing; the thing that
title: the act of doing
explain: Turns an action into a thing you can like, do, or talk about: 읽는 것 = reading.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 것, regardless of whether the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant (먹는 것, 가는 것). ㄹ-stem verbs drop ㄹ (만들다 → 만드는 것).

examples.en: I like reading books.

examples.ko: 여기에서 사진을 찍는 것은 안 돼요.
examples.en: Taking photos here is not allowed.
examples.rom: yeogieseo sajineul jjingneun geoseun an dwaeyo

note: 것 is often shortened to 거 in speech (먹는 거), and it can also mean 'the thing that'.

variants.title: the thing that was or will be

title: casual talk
explain: Drop 요 and talk casually to close friends or younger people: 뭐 해? = what are you doing?
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -아 if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise -어; this is the 해요체 form without 요. 하다 becomes 해.

examples.en: What are you doing now?
This food is really delicious.

note: Use it only with close friends, younger people or children; speaking banmal to a stranger or senior is rude.

title: is in a state
explain: Use -아/어 있다 to say something is now in a state after a change: 열려 있어요 = it's open.
attaches: Intransitive verb stem + -아 있다 if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise -어 있다 (앉아 있다, 열려 있다).

examples.en: The door is open.
The child is sitting on the chair.

note: It goes only with intransitive or passive verbs (앉다, 서다, 열리다). Transitive verbs use -아/어 놓다 instead.

title: plain written style
explain: Use -(느)ㄴ다/다 to state things plainly in diaries, essays, or books: 마신다 = I drink.
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄴ다 after a vowel (간다) or -는다 after a consonant (먹는다). Adjectives, 이다 and past stems take plain -다 (춥다, 갔다).

examples.en: I drink coffee in the morning.
The weather is very cold today.

note: This is the plain written style for diaries and essays. Adjectives never take -ㄴ다/는다. Do not use it when speaking to elders.

title: in doing, for doing
explain: Use -는 데 to say how much time or money it takes to do something: 끝내는 데 이틀 = two days to finish.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 데 (먹는 데, 만드는 데); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 데. 데 is a bound noun, so it is followed by a particle or a predicate such as 걸리다, 쓰이다, 도움이 되다.

examples.ko: 이 일을 끝내는 데 이틀이 걸려요.
examples.en: It takes two days to finish this work.
examples.rom: i ireul kkeunnaeneun de iteuri geollyeoyo

examples.en: These shoes are comfortable for walking.

note: Don't confuse the spaced noun 데 (-는 데) with the connective ending -(으)ㄴ/는데, which is written together.

meaning: be in the middle of doing
title: in the middle of
explain: Use -는 중이다 to say you're busy right in the middle of doing something: 회의하는 중이에요 = I'm in a meeting.

sample.en: I'm in the middle of doing it

attaches: Verb stem + -는 중이다, whether the stem ends in a vowel or a consonant. A ㄹ-stem drops ㄹ (만들다 → 만드는 중이다).

examples.en: I am in the middle of a meeting now.
I'm in the middle of preparing dinner.

note: It cannot be used with adjectives. It stresses that the action is in progress at this very moment.

title: whether, how, what
explain: Use -는지 inside a sentence to ask or say where, how, or whether: 어디에 사는지 = where (someone) lives.
attaches: Verb stem + -는지 (가는지, 먹는지); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ지 (예쁜지, 작은지); noun + -인지. For the past use -았/었는지.

examples.en: Do you know where that person lives?
I don't know what the weather will be like tomorrow.

note: It is used inside a sentence with verbs like 알다, 모르다, 묻다; in these questions use a question word or 'whether'.

meaning: did in the past (no longer true)
title: used to, but no more
explain: Use -았/었었- for something that was true in the past but isn't anymore: 살았었어요 = I used to live there.
attaches: Past stem + -았었- if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise -었었- (갔었어요, 먹었었어요). 하다 becomes 했었-.

examples.en: I used to live in Busan when I was young.
This cafe used to be quiet.

note: It implies the situation is no longer true or is cut off from the present. Do not use it for something that still continues.

title: as far as, the way
explain: A formal way to say what or how, often with knowing: 제가 아는 바로는 = as far as I know.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 바 (present), -(으)ㄴ 바 (past), -(으)ㄹ 바 (future); adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 바. 바 is a bound noun, so it is followed by a particle such as 로, 에 or 를.

examples.ko: 제가 아는 바로는 그 가게는 문을 닫았어요.
examples.en: As far as I know, that shop has closed.
examples.rom: jega aneun baroneun geu gageneun muneul dadasseoyo

examples.en: We proceed according to what was decided at the meeting.

note: It is formal and used in writing and speeches; don't use it for casual conversation.

title: used to, often do
explain: Add -곤 하다 after an action to say you did it again and again in the past: 가곤 했어요 = used to go.
attaches: Verb stem + -곤 하다, the same after a vowel or a consonant (가곤 하다, 먹곤 하다). It is a contraction of -고는 하다.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 주말마다 할머니 댁에 가곤 했어요.
examples.en: When I was little, I used to go to my grandmother's house every weekend.
examples.rom: eoril ttae jumalmada halmeoni daege gagon haesseoyo

examples.en: When I get stressed, I often listen to music.

note: Used only with verbs; with 했어요 it describes a past habit.

meaning: keep on doing, progress toward future
title: keep going, gradually
explain: Add -아/어 가다 to show something keeps going and moves toward the future: 늘어 가요 = it keeps growing.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 가다 after ㅏ/ㅗ, -어 가다 after other vowels, and 해 가다 for 하다 verbs.

examples.en: My Korean is gradually improving.

examples.ko: 이제 저녁 준비가 다 되어 가요.
examples.en: Dinner is almost ready now.
examples.rom: ije jeonyeok junbiga da doeeo gayo

note: It shows a process continuing from now toward the future; do not confuse it with the literal 'go after doing' meaning.

meaning: have been doing up to now
title: have been doing
explain: Use -아/어 오다 to say you have kept doing something from the past until now: 해 왔어요 = have been doing.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 오다 after ㅏ/ㅗ, -어 오다 after other vowels, and 해 오다 for 하다 verbs. It is often used in the past form (-아/어 왔다).

examples.ko: 저는 10년 동안 이 일을 해 왔어요.
examples.en: I have been doing this work for ten years.
examples.rom: jeoneun 10nyeon dongan i ireul hae wasseoyo

examples.ko: 우리는 오랫동안 이 문제를 고민해 왔어요.
examples.en: We have been worrying about this problem for a long time.
examples.rom: urineun oraetdongan i munjereul gominhae wasseoyo

note: It describes an action or state continuing from the past up to the present, usually with a time expression like 지금까지 or 동안.

title: by, using, towards
explain: Add N(으)로 after a noun to say how you do something or which way you go: 버스로 = by bus.
attaches: Noun + 으로 after a consonant (버스으로 is wrong; 손으로), 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로, 지하철로).

examples.en: I go to school by bus.
Please come this way.

note: After ㄹ, use 로 (지하철로), not 으로.

title: also, too
explain: Add N도 after a word to say 'also' or 'too': 저도 = me too.
attaches: Noun + 도 directly, regardless of the final sound; it replaces 이/가, 은/는, 을/를.

examples.en: I am a student too.
My friend likes movies too.

note: 도 replaces 이/가, 은/는, and 을/를, but it is added after 에, 에서, and (으)로 (학교에도).

title: to, at, on
explain: Add N에 after a place or time to say where you go or when something happens: 학교에 = to school.
attaches: Noun + 에 directly, regardless of the final sound; it attaches to places, destinations, and times.

examples.en: I go to school.
I wake up at seven o'clock.

note: 에 is used with existence and movement verbs (있다, 가다, 오다), while action places take 에서. Do not use 에 with 어제, 오늘, 지금.

title: to a person
explain: Add N에게/한테 after a person to say who receives something: 친구에게 = to my friend.
attaches: Noun (a person or animal) + 에게 or 한테 directly, regardless of the final sound.

examples.en: I give a present to my friend.
I called my younger sibling.

note: 에게/한테 is for people and animals, while 에 is for things and places (회사에 전화했어요). 한테 is more colloquial.

title: at, in, from
explain: Add N에서 after a place to say where you do something, or where you start from: 도서관에서 = at the library.
attaches: Noun + 에서 directly, regardless of the final sound; it attaches to places where actions happen or places of origin.

examples.en: I study at the library.
I came from Korea.

note: Use 에서 for where an action takes place, but 에 with 있다 (집에 있어요).

title: from place to place
explain: Use N에서 N까지 to say where a trip starts and ends: 집에서 학교까지 = from home to school.
attaches: Place noun + 에서, then place noun + 까지, with no change after vowels or consonants.

examples.ko: 집에서 학교까지 걸어서 십 분 걸려요.
examples.en: It takes ten minutes on foot from home to school.
examples.rom: jibeseo hakgyokkaji georeoseo sip bun geollyeoyo

examples.en: I go from Seoul to Busan by train.

note: Use 에서 … 까지 for places and 부터 … 까지 for times.

title: and, with
explain: Add N와/과 after a word to say 'and' or 'together with', common in writing or formal speech: 친구와 = with a friend.
attaches: Noun + 과 after a consonant (책과), 와 after a vowel (친구와).

examples.en: I watch a movie with a friend.
I bought bread and milk.

note: 와/과 is more formal and common in writing, while 하고 and (이)랑 are more conversational.

title: as for…
explain: Add N은/는 after a word to say 'as for this one', often to set it apart from others: 저는 = as for me.
attaches: Noun + 은 after a consonant (책은), 는 after a vowel (저는).

examples.en: I am a student.

examples.ko: 커피는 좋아해요. 하지만 차는 안 좋아해요.
examples.en: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.
examples.rom: keopineun joahaeyo hajiman chaneun an joahaeyo

note: 은/는 can mark contrast, so 커피는 좋아해요 implies something else is not liked.

title: marks what you act on
explain: Add N을/를 after the thing something is done to: 커피를 마셔요 = I drink coffee.
attaches: Noun + 을 after a consonant (책을), 를 after a vowel (커피를).

examples.en: I drink coffee.
My friend reads a book.

note: In speech 을/를 is often dropped, but it should be kept in careful writing. It is not used with 좋아하다-type verbs' opposite 좋다, which takes 이/가.

title: 's, of
explain: Add N의 between two nouns to show who something belongs to: 선생님의 책 = the teacher's book.
attaches: Noun + 의 directly, regardless of the final sound; it links the owner to the owned noun.

examples.en: This is the teacher's book.
I am going to my friend's house.

note: 의 is pronounced [에] when it is the possessive marker, and it is often dropped, as in 제 친구 or 우리 집.

title: who does it
explain: Add N이/가 after a person or thing to show who is doing something or being described: 친구가 = my friend (does it).
attaches: Noun + 이 after a consonant (학생이), 가 after a vowel (친구가).

examples.en: My friend is coming.
My younger sibling goes to school.

note: 이/가 introduces new information or the subject of a question word (누가 왔어요?), while 은/는 marks what is already known.

title: or
explain: Add N(이)나 between choices to say 'or': 영화나 드라마 = a movie or a drama.
attaches: Noun + 이나 after a consonant (빵이나), 나 after a vowel (커피나). For 'or', it joins two nouns (빵이나 밥); for 'as many as', it follows an amount.

examples.en: On weekends I watch a movie or a drama.
Yesterday I waited for my friend for as many as three hours.

note: After an amount, it means more than expected; do not use it for neutral quantities.

title: until, up to
explain: Add N까지 after a time or place to say where something ends: 여섯 시까지 = until six o'clock.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (오늘까지, 서울까지). It marks an endpoint of time or place, or 'even' for an extreme example.

examples.en: I work until six in the afternoon.
He even knows my name.

note: 까지 marks the end point and 부터 marks the start; the 'even' meaning adds something beyond what was expected.

title: during, for
explain: Add N동안 after a time word to say how long something lasts: 방학 동안 = during vacation.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun of time or duration, after a vowel or a consonant (방학 동안, 세 시간 동안). It is usually written with a space.

examples.en: I stayed in Korea during the vacation.
I studied for two hours.

note: Use it with nouns; with verbs use -는 동안 instead.

title: every, each
explain: Add N마다 after a time word to say 'every' one: 주말마다 = every weekend.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (날마다, 주말마다). It is mostly used with time words and with nouns for people or places.

examples.en: I exercise every weekend.
Every house has a garden.

note: The noun is singular and stands for 'each one'; do not add 을/를 after 마다.

title: only
explain: Add N만 after a word to say 'only that and nothing else': 커피만 = only coffee.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (물만, 너만). It can be followed by other particles (너한테만, 집에서만).

examples.en: I drink only coffee.
My younger sibling does nothing but play games.

note: It replaces 이/가 and 을/를 (책을만 is wrong), but it stacks after 에, 에서, 에게 and similar particles.

title: from, since
explain: Add N부터 after a time or thing to say where something begins: 아침부터 = since morning.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (아침부터, 이것부터). It marks the starting point of time or order.

examples.en: It has been raining since morning.
Please start by eating this first.

note: For a starting place use 에서, not 부터, unless it means 'starting with' in a sequence.

title: from a person
explain: Add N에게서/한테서 after a person to say who you got something from: 친구한테서 = from a friend.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun for a person (or animal), after a vowel or a consonant (친구에게서, 친구한테서). 한테서 is more colloquial than 에게서.

examples.en: I received a present from my friend.
I heard this story from my mother.

note: It is used only for people or animals; for places use N에서. In speech, 한테 alone often replaces 한테서 with verbs like 받다 and 듣다.

title: about, around
explain: Add N쯤 after a time or amount to say it is approximate: 세 시쯤 = around three o'clock.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun of time, number, or amount, after a vowel or a consonant (세 시쯤, 열 명쯤). It is used for rough estimates.

examples.en: Let's meet around three o'clock tomorrow afternoon.
It takes about ten minutes from here to school.

note: It is used with specific numbers or times; do not combine it with other approximating words like 약 for the same estimate.

title: at least, even just
explain: Add N(이)라도 after a word to suggest a modest option when the ideal isn't possible: 커피라도 = at least a coffee.
attaches: Noun + 이라도 after a consonant (밥이라도), 라도 after a vowel (커피라도). It suggests a second-best choice or the least one can do.

examples.en: If you have no time, at least have a cup of coffee.
If you are busy, please at least call.

note: It implies the noun is not ideal but acceptable, so it is not used for a first choice.

title: just as, according to
explain: Add N대로 after a word to say something happens exactly the way it was said or planned: 계획대로 = as planned.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun with no space (약속대로, 계획대로), with no change after a vowel or a consonant.

examples.en: The work is going well, just as planned.
Please do as I told you.

note: As a particle, 대로 is attached to the noun; after a verb ending like -는/-(으)ㄴ it is a separate word (-는 대로).

title: only (nothing but)
explain: Add N밖에 after a word, then use a 'not/none' ending, to say there is only that much: 천 원밖에 없어요 = only 1,000 won.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun (usually an amount), after a vowel or a consonant (하나밖에, 천 원밖에). It must be followed by a negative predicate.

examples.en: I have only 1,000 won now.
I can speak only a little Korean.

note: 밖에 always needs a negative verb (없다, 안, 못); with an affirmative verb use N만.

title: about, regarding
explain: Add N에 대해(서) after a word to say what you are talking, studying or thinking about: 역사에 대해 = about history.
attaches: Attaches to a noun with no change after a vowel or a consonant (한국 문화에 대해). Before a noun it becomes N에 대한 N.

examples.en: I am studying about Korean history.
What do you think about this problem?

note: Before a noun use 에 대한 (한국에 대한 책), not 에 대해.

title: for the sake of
explain: Add N을/를 위해(서) after a word to say who or what you do something for: 가족을 위해 = for my family.
attaches: Noun + 을 after a consonant (가족을 위해), 를 after a vowel (친구를 위해), then 위해(서).

examples.en: I work hard for my family.
I exercise every day for my health.

note: 위해 shows purpose or benefit, not cause; use 때문에 for a cause.

title: as (in the role of)
explain: Add N(으)로서 after a word to say in what role or position someone does something: 학생으로서 = as a student.
attaches: Noun + 으로서 after a consonant (학생으로서), 로서 after a vowel or ㄹ (부모로서, 선생님으로서 stays 으로서 after ㅁ? no: 교사로서).

examples.en: As a student, I should study hard.
As a parent, I worry about my child.

note: 으로서 marks status or capacity (as a student); do not confuse with 으로써, which marks a means.

title: by means of, with
explain: Add N(으)로써 after a word to say the tool or method used to do something: 대화로써 = by means of conversation.
attaches: Noun + 으로써 after a consonant (말로써 is ㄹ so 로써), 로써 after a vowel or ㄹ (대화로써), 으로써 after other consonants (노력으로써).

examples.en: You can solve the problem by means of conversation.
I achieved my dream through effort.

note: 로써 marks a tool or means; do not confuse it with 로서 (status).

title: any, whichever
explain: Add N(이)든지 after a word to say any one at all will do: 누구든지 = anyone.
attaches: Noun + 이든지 after a consonant (무엇이든지), 든지 after a vowel (누구든지).

examples.ko: 누구든지 이 방에 들어올 수 있어요.
examples.en: Anyone can enter this room.
examples.rom: nugudeunji i bange deureool su isseoyo

examples.en: Tell me anything.

note: Usually used with question words (누구, 뭐, 언제, 어디) to mean any-; 든지 is often shortened to 든.

title: depending on
explain: Add N에 따라(서) after a word to say the result changes with it: 사람에 따라 = depending on the person.
attaches: Attaches to a noun with no change after a vowel or a consonant (사람에 따라). Before a noun it becomes N에 따른 N.

examples.en: Thoughts differ depending on the person.
My mood changes depending on the weather.

note: Often paired with words like 다르다 or 달라지다 to show variation.

title: through, via
explain: Add N을/를 통해(서) after a word to say the person or way something came through: 친구를 통해 = through a friend.
attaches: Noun + 을 after a consonant (경험을 통해), 를 after a vowel (친구를 통해), then 통해(서).

examples.en: I heard the news through a friend.
I learned many things through books.

note: Before a noun it becomes N을/를 통한 N.

title: even (not even)
explain: Add N조차 after a word to stress that even something basic is not possible: 밥조차 = not even a meal.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (이름조차).

examples.en: I was so busy I couldn't even eat a meal.
That person doesn't even know my name.

note: 조차 is normally used with a negative predicate and suggests that something expected is lacking.

title: for a, considering
explain: Add N치고 after a word to say how someone is surprising for that group: 학생치고 = for a student.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (학생치고).

examples.en: For a student, he doesn't study well.
You speak Korean well for a foreigner.

note: 치고 often introduces a general rule about a class, with the second clause stating something against or in line with expectation.

title: shall we…?
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ까요? to suggest doing something together or offer to do something: 볼까요? = shall we watch?
attaches: Verb stem + -을까요? after a consonant (먹을까요?), -ㄹ까요? after a vowel (갈까요?); ㄹ-stem verbs drop ㄹ before ㄹ (만들까요?).

examples.en: Shall we watch a movie together this weekend?
Shall I open the door?

note: With 우리 or an implied 'we' it is a suggestion; with 제가 it offers to do something.

title: please do / polite
explain: Add -(으)세요 to an action word to politely ask someone to do something or to say what an older person does: 읽으세요 = please read.
attaches: Verb stem + -세요 after a vowel (가세요), -으세요 after a consonant (읽으세요). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 사세요).

examples.en: My mother is reading a book now.
Please sit here.

note: Some verbs use special honorific forms, such as 드세요 (먹다/마시다), 주무세요 (자다) and 계세요 (있다).

title: formal polite question
explain: Put -ㅂ니까?/습니까? at the end of an action or description to ask a question formally: 갑니까? = are you going?
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -ㅂ니까 after a vowel (갑니까), -습니까 after a consonant (먹습니까). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 삽니까).

examples.en: Where are you going?
Did you eat lunch?

note: Used only for questions in formal situations; it sounds stiff in everyday conversation.

title: please do for me
explain: Use -아/어 주세요 to ask someone to do something for you: 열어 주세요 = please open it for me.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 주세요 after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (찾아 주세요), -어 주세요 otherwise (읽어 주세요); 하다 becomes 해 주세요.

examples.en: Please open the window for me.
Please explain the meaning of this word to me.

note: Use it to ask someone to do something for you; it is not used when you offer to do something yourself (use -아/어 드릴까요?).

meaning: do you want to…? / will you…?
title: do you want to…?
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ래요? to ask if someone wants to do something, or to say what you want to do: 마실래요? = want to drink?
attaches: Verb stem + -을래요? after a consonant (먹을래요?), -ㄹ래요? after a vowel (갈래요?); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before attaching (놀다 → 놀래요?).

examples.en: Do you want to drink coffee?
Do you want to watch a movie with me?

note: It asks about the listener's wish and is casual, so it is not suitable for superiors; in statements it means 'I want to' (저는 안 갈래요).

title: shall I do it for you?
explain: Use -아/어 드릴까요? to offer help: 들어 드릴까요? = shall I carry it for you?

sample.en: shall I carry it for you?

attaches: Verb stem + -아 드릴까요? after ㅏ/ㅗ (도와 드릴까요?), -어 드릴까요? after other vowels (열어 드릴까요?); 하다 becomes 해 드릴까요?.

examples.en: That looks heavy. Shall I carry it for you?
Shall I open the window for you?

note: It offers help to someone you respect; do not use it for asking others to do something for you.

title: please try doing
explain: Use -아/어 보세요 to invite someone to try something out: 먹어 보세요 = please try eating it.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 보세요 after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (가 보세요), -어 보세요 otherwise (먹어 보세요); 하다 becomes 해 보세요.

examples.en: Please try this kimchi.
Please try looking up words you don't know in a dictionary.

note: It suggests trying something as an experience, so it is not a plain command like -(으)세요.

title: would you please…?
explain: Use -아/어 주시겠어요? to ask a favor very politely: 찍어 주시겠어요? = would you please take it?
attaches: Verb stem + -아 주시겠어요? after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (도와 주시겠어요?), -어 주시겠어요? otherwise (읽어 주시겠어요?); 하다 becomes 해 주시겠어요?.

examples.en: Excuse me, would you please take a photo for me?
Would you please wait a moment?

note: A more polite, indirect request than -아/어 주세요, suited to strangers and superiors.

title: let's
explain: Use -자 with friends or people younger than you to suggest doing something together: 먹자 = let's eat.
attaches: Verb stem + -자, with no change for vowels or consonants (가자, 먹자); used with action verbs only.

examples.en: Let's eat dinner together tonight.
The weather is nice, so let's go to the park.

note: This is informal 반말 for close friends or juniors, so avoid it with elders; the polite form is -아요/어요 or -(으)ㅂ시다.

title: right? isn't it?
explain: Add -지요?/죠? to check if someone agrees or to say something you both know: 좋지요? = it's good, right?
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -지요 (often contracted to -죠), with no change for vowels or consonants. Past is -았/었지요, and with 이다 it is 이지요/이죠.

examples.en: The weather is nice today, isn't it?
You'll go together tomorrow, right?

note: It seeks agreement or confirmation of something the speaker already assumes; with falling intonation it can be a gentle statement.

title: would you like to?
explain: Use -(으)시겠어요? to politely offer something or ask what someone wants to do: 드시겠어요? = would you like to eat?
attaches: Verb stem + -으시겠어요 after a consonant (드시겠어요), -시겠어요 after a vowel (가시겠어요).

examples.en: Would you like some coffee?
Would you like to sit and wait for a moment?

note: It is honorific and is only used for the listener's action. Never use it about yourself.

title: how about doing…?
explain: Use -는 게 어때요? to suggest an idea: 자는 게 어때요? = how about sleeping?
attaches: Verb stem + -는 게 어때요? regardless of final sound (가는 게 어때요?, 먹는 게 어때요?); ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (만들다 → 만드는 게 어때요?).

examples.en: How about going to bed early today?
How about taking a taxi?

note: It is a soft suggestion to the listener; it can be said about a single action, not necessarily done together.

title: why don't you…?
explain: Use -지 그래요? to suggest something to someone, often when they seem tired or stuck: 쉬지 그래요? = why don't you rest?
attaches: Verb stem + -지 그래요? regardless of final sound (가지 그래요?, 먹지 그래요?).

examples.en: If you're tired, why don't you rest a bit?
Why don't you ask him directly?

note: It can sound mildly critical or pushy; it suggests an action the listener hasn't taken yet.

title: why don't we…?
explain: Use -지 않을래요? to gently invite someone to do something together: 같이 가지 않을래요? = why don't we go together?
attaches: Verb stem + -지 않을래요? regardless of final sound (가지 않을래요?, 먹지 않을래요?).

examples.en: Why don't we go hiking together this weekend?
Why don't we have lunch?

note: The negative form makes the invitation softer and more polite than -(으)ㄹ래요?.

title: soft question
explain: Add -(으)ㄴ가요?/나요? to ask a gentle, polite question: 바쁜가요? = are you busy?
attaches: Adjective or 이다 stem + -(으)ㄴ가요 (바쁜가요, 학생인가요). Verb stem + -나요 (가나요, 먹나요), and the past form is -았/었나요.

examples.en: Are you very busy these days?
Does this bus go to City Hall?

note: It sounds softer and less direct than -아요/어요 questions. A verb takes -나요, not -(으)ㄴ가요, in the present.

title: please make sure to
explain: Use -도록 하세요 to firmly but politely tell someone to be sure to do something: 늦지 않도록 하세요 = make sure not to be late.
attaches: Verb stem + -도록 하세요 regardless of final sound (가도록 하세요, 먹도록 하세요).

examples.en: Please make sure you are not late tomorrow.
Please make sure to take your medicine.

note: It is a soft but firm instruction usually from a superior or expert; it is not suited to speaking up to a superior.

title: will / going to
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 to say your plans or what will happen: 만날 거예요 = I'm going to meet.
attaches: Verb stem + -을 거예요 after a consonant (먹을 거예요), -ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel (갈 거예요). A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ (살 거예요), and ㅂ-irregular stems change (도우다 → 도울 거예요).

examples.en: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
I will rest at home this weekend.

note: With a third-person subject it can also mean a guess ('probably will').

title: to go and do
explain: Add -(으)러 before 가요/와요 to say the purpose of going or coming: 만나러 = to meet.
attaches: Verb stem + -으러 after a consonant (먹으러), -러 after a vowel or ㄹ (만나러, 놀러). It is followed by a movement verb such as 가다, 오다 or 다니다.

examples.en: I am going to meet a friend.
I am going to a restaurant to eat lunch.

note: It works only before movement verbs, but it can be used with commands and suggestions, unlike -(으)려고.

title: want to
explain: Add -고 싶다 to an action to say what you yourself want to do: 가고 싶어요 = I want to go.
attaches: Verb stem + -고 싶다, regardless of a final consonant (먹고 싶다, 가고 싶다).

examples.en: I want to go to Korea.
Today I want to rest at home.

note: It is used for the speaker's own wish in statements and for the listener in questions; for a third person use -고 싶어 하다.

title: try doing
explain: Add -아/어 보다 to an action to say you try it out and see: 입어 봤어요 = I tried it on.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 보다 if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (가 보다, 와 보다), otherwise -어 보다 (먹어 보다); 하다 becomes 해 보다.

examples.ko: 저는 이 옷을 한번 입어 봤어요.
examples.en: I tried on this outfit once.
examples.rom: jeoneun i oseul hanbeon ibeo bwasseoyo

examples.en: I'll try making Korean food.

note: It attaches to action verbs, not adjectives; 보다 here means 'try', not 'see'.

title: have done before
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 to say you have or have never done something in your life: 간 적이 있어요 = I have been there.
attaches: Verb stem + -은 적이 있다/없다 after a consonant (먹은 적), -ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 after a vowel (간 적). ㄹ-final stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 산 적).

examples.en: I have been to Jeju Island.

examples.ko: 저는 그 영화를 본 적이 없어요.
examples.en: I have never seen that movie.
examples.rom: jeoneun geu yeonghwareul bon jeogi eopseoyo

note: It refers to past experience and attaches only to verbs; for an experience of trying something, -아/어 본 적이 있다 is more common.

title: I'll do it
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ게요 to promise or tell the listener what you decide to do: 갈게요 = I'll go.
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄹ게요 after a vowel (갈게요), -을게요 after a consonant (먹을게요). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (만들다 → 만들게요); it attaches only to verbs.

examples.en: I'll go first.
I'll call you tomorrow.

note: The subject must be the speaker, and it cannot be used as a question or with adjectives.

title: in order to
explain: Use -(으)려고 to say your aim or plan behind an action: 일하려고 = in order to work.
attaches: Verb stem + -으려고 after a consonant (먹으려고), -려고 after a vowel or ㄹ (사려고, 놀려고).

examples.en: I am learning Korean in order to work in Korea.
I went to the department store to buy a present.

note: Both clauses share the same subject, and the second clause cannot be a command or suggestion.

title: plan to, about to
explain: Use -(으)려고 하다 to say what you intend to do or are just about to do: 영화를 보려고 해요 = I plan to watch a movie.
attaches: Verb stem + -려고 하다 after a vowel (가려고 하다), -으려고 하다 after a consonant (먹으려고 하다).

examples.en: I intend to watch a movie this weekend.
I was about to leave now, but a call came.

note: Used with verbs only; the past form -(으)려고 했다 often means 'was about to' or 'had intended to'.

title: he/she wants to
explain: Use -고 싶어 하다 to say what another person wants to do, not yourself: 가고 싶어 해요 = he or she wants to go.
attaches: Verb stem + -고 싶어 하다, regardless of a final consonant (먹고 싶어 하다, 가고 싶어 하다).

examples.en: My younger sibling wants to become a singer.
The children want to go to the amusement park.

note: Use it for a third person's wish; plain -고 싶다 is normally for the speaker's own feelings.

title: scheduled to
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 예정이다 to say something is planned on a schedule: 이사할 예정이에요 = I'm scheduled to move.
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄹ 예정이다 after a vowel, -을 예정이다 after a consonant; a noun can also be used directly (N 예정이다).

examples.en: I'm scheduled to move next week.
The meeting is scheduled to start at three.

note: It implies a schedule or arrangement, so it fits formal or official contexts.

title: thinking of doing
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ까 하다 to say you are considering doing something but haven't fully decided: 갈까 해요 = I'm thinking of going.
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄹ까 하다 after a vowel (갈까 하다), -을까 하다 after a consonant (먹을까 하다).

examples.en: I'm thinking of going to Jeju Island on this vacation.
I'm thinking of resting at home this evening.

note: It is less decided than -(으)려고 하다; the subject is normally the speaker.

meaning: I wish; it would be nice if
title: I hope; it'd be nice if
explain: Use -(으)면 좋겠다 to say what you wish would happen or be true: 날씨가 좋으면 좋겠어요 = I hope the weather is nice.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -으면 좋겠다 after a consonant (먹으면 좋겠어요), -면 좋겠다 after a vowel (오면 좋겠어요).

examples.en: I hope the weather is nice tomorrow.
It would be nice if we could watch a movie together this weekend.

note: It expresses a wish about something that may still happen; -았/었으면 좋겠다 often sounds a little stronger or more unlikely.

meaning: so that; in a way that
title: so that
explain: Use -게 to say how you do something so a result follows: 잘 들리게 = so that it can be heard well.

sample.en: so it can be heard well

attaches: Adjective or verb stem + -게, with no change for final consonants. It turns an adjective into an adverb or expresses purpose or result.

examples.ko: 모두가 잘 들리게 크게 말해 주세요.
examples.en: Please speak loudly so that everyone can hear well.
examples.rom: moduga jal deullige keuge malhae juseyo

examples.en: I stay quiet so that the child does not wake up.

note: As a purpose marker, the two clauses can have different subjects, unlike -(으)려고.

title: decide to
explain: Use -기로 하다 to say you decided or agreed to do something: 만나기로 했어요 = we decided to meet.
attaches: Verb stem + -기로 하다 after both vowels and consonants (가기로 하다, 먹기로 하다).

examples.en: I decided to meet my friend tomorrow.
I decided to exercise starting this year.

note: It expresses a decision or agreement already made, so it is usually in the past tense (-기로 했어요).

title: after trying, I found
explain: Use -아/어 보니(까) to share what you discovered after trying something: 먹어 보니까 맛있었어요 = I tried it and it was tasty.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 보니(까) if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise -어 보니(까) (먹어 보니까); 하다 becomes 해 보니(까).

examples.en: When I actually tried eating it, it was really delicious.
After living in Korea, I found it more comfortable than I expected.

note: The main clause states a discovery, so it normally cannot be a command or suggestion.

title: was just about to
explain: Use -(으)려던 참이다 to say you were right on the point of doing something when something else happened: 하려던 참이에요 = I was just about to do it.

sample.en: I was just about to go

attaches: Verb stem + -으려던 참이다 after a consonant (먹으려던 참이에요), -려던 참이다 after a vowel (가려던 참이에요).

examples.en: I was just about to call you.
I was just about to eat lunch too.

note: It means the action was about to start at that very moment, not a general plan.

title: hope that
explain: Use -기(를) 바라다 to wish good things for someone: 잘 보기를 바라요 = I hope you do well.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -기를 바라다, regardless of a final consonant (먹기를 바라요, 가기를 바라요). The 를 can be dropped.

examples.en: I hope you do well on the exam.
I wish that everyone be happy.

note: It is rather formal; 바라요 and 바랍니다 are common in speeches, letters and notices.

meaning: in the course of doing, I found that
title: as I kept doing
explain: Use -다가 보니(까) to say that by continuing an action, you noticed or got a result: 운동하다가 보니 = as I kept exercising.
attaches: Verb stem + -다가 보니(까), regardless of final consonant or vowel (하다가 보니, 먹다가 보니까).

examples.en: As I kept exercising every day, I became healthier.

examples.ko: 한국어를 공부하다가 보니까 한국 문화에도 관심이 생겼어요.
examples.en: As I kept studying Korean, I also became interested in Korean culture.
examples.rom: hangugeoreul gongbuhadaga bonikka hanguk munhwaedo gwansimi saenggyeosseoyo

note: It implies a repeated or continued action that leads to a realization; -다가 보면 is the 'if you keep doing' version.

meaning: even if one tries, it is no use
title: no use even if
explain: Use -아/어 봤자 to say that doing something will not help: 가 봤자 = even if you go, it's no use.

sample.en: even if you go, no use

attaches: Verb stem + -아 봤자 if the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ (가 봤자), otherwise -어 봤자 (먹어 봤자); 하다 becomes 해 봤자.

examples.ko: 지금 가 봤자 문이 닫혀 있을 거예요.
examples.en: Even if you go now, it will be closed.
examples.rom: jigeum ga bwatja muni datyeo isseul geoyeyo

examples.en: Even if you tell him, it's no use.

note: The following clause is negative or futile (소용없다, 마찬가지다), and it cannot end in a command or suggestion.

title: can, cannot
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 to say you are able or not able to do something: 먹을 수 있어요 = I can eat.
attaches: Verb stem + -을 수 있다/없다 after a consonant (먹을 수 있어요), -ㄹ 수 있다/없다 after a vowel (갈 수 있어요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (만들 수 있어요), and ㄷ-irregulars change to ㄹ (들을 수 있어요).

examples.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 있어요.
examples.en: I can eat spicy food.
examples.rom: jeoneun maeun eumsigeul meogeul su isseoyo

examples.en: I'm busy today, so I can't go.

note: It covers both ability and possibility or permission; the subject is marked with 이/가 on 수 only in special cases.

title: must not
explain: Use -(으)면 안 되다 to say something is not allowed: 말하면 안 돼요 = you must not speak.
attaches: Verb stem + -으면 안 되다 after a consonant (먹으면 안 되다), -면 안 되다 after a vowel (가면 안 되다). ㄹ-final stems drop ㄹ before ㅁ-type endings? No, they just add 면 (놀면 안 되다).

examples.ko: 도서관에서 큰 소리로 말하면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not speak loudly in the library.
examples.rom: doseogwaneseo keun soriro malhamyeon an dwaeyo

examples.ko: 수업 시간에 휴대폰을 보면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You must not look at your phone during class.
examples.rom: sueop sigane hyudaeponeul bomyeon an dwaeyo

note: It states a rule or prohibition; it is the natural negative answer to -아도/어도 돼요?.

title: may; it's okay to
explain: Use -아도/어도 되다 to ask or give permission: 찍어도 돼요? = may I take it?
attaches: Verb stem + -아도 되다 after ㅏ or ㅗ (가도 되다 uses 가 → 가도), -어도 되다 after other vowels (먹어도 되다), and 해도 되다 for 하다 verbs.

examples.en: May I take photos here?
You may go home now.

note: Asking 먹어도 돼요? is a request for permission; 괜찮아요 is a softer alternative.

title: please don't
explain: Use -지 마세요 to politely ask someone not to do something: 버리지 마세요 = please don't throw it away.
attaches: Verb stem + -지 마세요, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (가지 마세요, 먹지 마세요). It attaches to verbs only, not adjectives.

examples.en: Please don't throw trash here.
Please don't worry too much.

note: Do not use 안 or -지 않으세요 for a request not to do something; use -지 마세요.

title: can't (short way)
explain: Put 못 before an action to say you can't do it: 못 가요 = I can't go.
attaches: Place 못 directly before a verb (못 가요, 못 먹어요). With 하다 verbs, put 못 before 하다 (공부 못 해요).

examples.en: I'm too busy today, so I can't go.
I can't swim.

note: Do not use 못 with adjectives; also, 못 is not a command form, so 못 가세요 is not 'don't go' (that is 가지 마세요).

meaning: know how to / not know how to
title: know how to
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다 to say you have a learned skill: 쓸 줄 알아요 = I know how to write.
attaches: Verb stem + -을 줄 알다/모르다 after a consonant (읽을 줄 알아요), -ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다 after a vowel (탈 줄 몰라요). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (만들 줄 알아요).

examples.ko: 저는 한국어로 편지를 쓸 줄 알아요.
examples.en: I know how to write a letter in Korean.
examples.rom: jeoneun hangugeoro pyeonjireul sseul jul arayo

examples.en: My younger sibling doesn't know how to ride a bike.

note: It is about learned skill (know how to), not mere possibility; do not confuse it with -는 줄 알다 ('think that').

meaning: it is enough if; all you need to do is
title: all you need to do
explain: Use -(으)면 되다 to say that doing just one thing is enough: 누르면 돼요 = all you need to do is press.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -으면 되다 after a consonant (먹으면 되다), -면 되다 after a vowel (가면 되다). ㄹ-final stems add -면 directly (살면 되다).

examples.en: All you need to do is press this button.
It is enough if you come by tomorrow morning.

note: It gives the minimum condition; do not confuse it with -아야/어야 되다 (must).

title: have to
explain: Use -아야/어야 하다 to say something must be done or should be done: 일어나야 해요 = I have to get up.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -아야 하다 after ㅏ or ㅗ (가야 하다), -어야 하다 after other vowels (먹어야 하다), 해야 하다 for 하다.

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You must take the medicine every day.

note: Past is 해야 했어요, not 해야 하았어요; -아야/어야 되다 is a common, slightly more casual equivalent.

title: need to / no need to
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다 to say whether something is needed: 할 필요가 없어요 = there's no need to do it.
attaches: Verb stem + -을 필요가 있다/없다 after a consonant (읽을 필요가 있다), -ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다 after a vowel (갈 필요가 없다).

examples.ko: 이 일은 지금 당장 할 필요가 없어요.
examples.en: There is no need to do this right now.
examples.rom: i ireun jigeum dangjang hal pillyoga eopseoyo

examples.ko: 발표 전에 자료를 한 번 더 확인할 필요가 있어요.
examples.en: You need to check the materials once more before the presentation.
examples.rom: balpyo jeone jaryoreul han beon deo hwaginhal pillyoga isseoyo

note: With 없다 it means 'no need to', not 'must not'; for prohibition use -(으)면 안 되다.

title: easy to do
explain: Use -기 쉽다 to say an action is easy, or likely to happen: 읽기 쉬워요 = it's easy to read.
attaches: Verb stem + -기 쉽다, regardless of a final consonant (먹기 쉬워요, 넘어지기 쉬워요). 쉽다 is ㅂ-irregular: 쉬워요.

examples.en: This book is easy to read.
In winter, it's easy to catch a cold.

note: It can mean either 'easy to do' or 'apt to happen', depending on the context.

title: hard to do
explain: Use -기 어렵다 to say an action is difficult: 읽기 어려워요 = it's hard to read.
attaches: Verb stem + -기 (no change after a vowel or a consonant), followed by 어렵다: 먹기 어렵다, 가기 어렵다.

examples.ko: 이 책은 내용이 많아서 읽기 어려워요.
examples.en: This book has a lot of content, so it is hard to read.
examples.rom: i chaegeun naeyongi manaseo ikgi eoryeowoyo

examples.en: That person's feelings are hard to understand.

note: 어렵다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective (어려워요). The subject of the sentence is usually the object of the verb (the thing that is hard to do).

title: it would be better
explain: Use -는 게 좋겠다 to gently suggest the better choice: 가져가는 게 좋겠어요 = it would be better to take it.

sample.en: it would be better to go

attaches: Verb stem + -는 게 좋겠다 with no change for vowels or consonants (가는 게 좋겠다, 먹는 게 좋겠다).

examples.ko: 비가 오니까 우산을 가져가는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.en: It's raining, so it would be better to take an umbrella.
examples.rom: biga onikka usaneul gajyeoganeun ge jokesseoyo

examples.ko: 감기에 걸렸으면 오늘은 집에서 쉬는 게 좋겠어요.
examples.en: If you have a cold, it would be better to rest at home today.
examples.rom: gamgie geollyeosseumyeon oneureun jibeseo swineun ge jokesseoyo

note: A soft way to give advice; 게 is the contraction of 것이.

title: I'd better
explain: Use -아야/어야겠다 to say what you decide you should do, often for yourself: 자야겠어요 = I'd better sleep.
attaches: Verb stem + -아야겠다 after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (가야겠다), -어야겠다 otherwise (먹어야겠다); 하다 becomes 해야겠다.

examples.en: I'm so tired that I'd better go to bed early today.

examples.ko: 시험이 다음 주라서 이제 공부를 시작해야겠어요.
examples.en: The exam is next week, so I should start studying now.
examples.rom: siheomi daeum juraseo ije gongbureul sijakaeyagesseoyo

note: Expresses the speaker's own decision or resolve; it is not used for ordering others.

title: no way that
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 to say you strongly doubt something is true: 할 리가 없어요 = there's no way he'd do it.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 리가 없다 after a consonant (먹을 리가 없다), -ㄹ 리가 없다 after a vowel (갈 리가 없다). ㄹ-final stems just add 리가 없다 (살 리가 없다).

examples.ko: 그 친구가 거짓말을 할 리가 없어요.
examples.en: There is no way that friend would tell a lie.
examples.rom: geu chinguga geojinmareul hal riga eopseoyo

examples.ko: 어제 산 옷이 벌써 작을 리가 없어요.
examples.en: There is no way the clothes I bought yesterday are already too small.
examples.rom: eoje san osi beolsseo jageul riga eopseoyo

note: It expresses the speaker's strong belief that something is impossible, not a lack of ability or permission.

title: worth doing
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 만하다 to say something is good enough to be worth doing: 볼 만해요 = it's worth watching.
attaches: Verb stem + -을 만하다 after a consonant (먹을 만하다), -ㄹ 만하다 after a vowel (볼 만하다).

examples.en: This movie is worth watching once.
Jeju Island is a place worth traveling to.

note: Do not confuse it with 만 (only); 만하다 is written with a space as 만 하다 only in older style, but standard spelling is 만하다.

title: no choice but to
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 to say something is the only option left: 있을 수밖에 없어요 = I have no choice but to stay.

sample.en: I have no choice but to go

attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 수밖에 없다 after a consonant (먹을 수밖에 없다), -ㄹ 수밖에 없다 after a vowel (갈 수밖에 없다).

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와서 집에 있을 수밖에 없어요.
examples.en: It is raining a lot, so I have no choice but to stay home.
examples.rom: biga mani waseo jibe isseul subakke eopseoyo

examples.ko: 시험이 내일이라서 오늘 밤새 공부할 수밖에 없어요.
examples.en: The exam is tomorrow, so I have no choice but to study all night tonight.
examples.rom: siheomi naeiriraseo oneul bamsae gongbuhal subakke eopseoyo

note: 밖에 here is followed by a negative (없다); the whole phrase is not the same as 수 없다 (cannot).

title: make or let someone
explain: Use -게 하다 to say you make or let someone do something: 읽게 했어요 = made (them) read.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -게 하다 with no change after a vowel or a consonant (가게 하다, 먹게 하다).

examples.en: The teacher made the students read a book.
The parents make the child go to bed early.

note: The context decides between 'make' and 'let'; the person made to act is marked with 에게/한테 or 을/를.

meaning: is bound to; naturally tends to
title: bound to
explain: Use -기 마련이다 to say something naturally happens or is sure to happen: 실수하기 마련이에요 = (people) are bound to make mistakes.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -기 마련이다, with no change for vowels or consonants (늙기 마련이다, 변하기 마련이다).

examples.en: Everyone is bound to make mistakes.
As time passes, memories naturally tend to fade.

note: Describes a natural or general truth, not a one-time event or personal obligation.

meaning: manage to do; accomplish through effort
title: manage to do
explain: Use -아/어 내다 to say you finished something difficult through effort: 참아 냈어요 = I managed to endure it.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 내다 after the vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (찾아 내다), -어 내다 after other vowels (참아 내다 is ㅏ; 이겨 내다 is 이기다 → 이겨). Use the 해 form for 하다 verbs (해 내다).

examples.en: It was hard, but I managed to endure it to the end.

examples.ko: 그 학생은 어려운 문제를 혼자 풀어 냈어요.
examples.en: That student managed to solve the difficult problem alone.
examples.rom: geu haksaengeun eoryeoun munjereul honja pureo naesseoyo

note: It implies effort and difficulty overcome, so it sounds odd with easy, effortless actions.

title: can't help but
explain: Use -지 않을 수 없다 to say you can't stop yourself from doing something: 웃지 않을 수 없어요 = I can't help laughing.
attaches: Verb stem + -지 않을 수 없다, with no change for vowels or consonants (웃지 않을 수 없다, 가지 않을 수 없다).

examples.ko: 그 이야기를 들으면 웃지 않을 수 없어요.
examples.en: When you hear that story, you can't help laughing.
examples.rom: geu iyagireul deureumyeon utji aneul su eopseoyo

examples.ko: 상황이 이러니 그 제안을 받아들이지 않을 수 없어요.
examples.en: Given the situation, I can't help but accept that offer.
examples.rom: sanghwangi ireoni geu jeaneul badadeuriji aneul su eopseoyo

note: A double negative that means 'must/cannot but'; it is a bit formal and often used for reluctant necessity.

title: and, and then
explain: Join two actions in order or list things: 먹고 가요 = eat and go.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -고, the same after a vowel or a consonant. Tense goes on the final verb only.

examples.en: I eat breakfast and go to school.
My younger sibling is tall and I am short.

note: Put tense only on the last clause (먹고 갔어요), not on -고 itself.

title: before doing
explain: Use -기 전에 to say what you do ahead of another action: 자기 전에 = before sleeping.
attaches: Verb stem + -기 전에, the same after a vowel or a consonant; with nouns use N 전에.

examples.en: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
I learned Korean before coming to Korea.

note: Do not put a past tense before 전에: say 먹기 전에, not 먹었기 전에.

title: and then
explain: Use -아서/어서 when the first action leads into the next one: 만나서 봤어요 = met and then watched.
attaches: Verb stem + -아서 after ㅏ/ㅗ, -어서 after other vowels, and 해서 for 하다 verbs. 가다 and 오다 usually appear as 가서 and 와서.

examples.en: I met a friend and then watched a movie.
I went to the library and borrowed a book.

note: The two actions are closely connected and share the same subject; do not put -았/었- before -아서/어서.

title: after doing
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ 후에 to say something happens after an action is finished: 먹은 후에 = after eating.
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄴ 후에 after a vowel, -은 후에 after a consonant (먹은 후에). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 논 후에).

examples.en: I drink coffee after eating.
I'll call you after class ends.

note: Used with verbs only; the tense is shown on the final verb.

title: while doing
explain: Say you do two things at the same time: 들으면서 공부해요 = study while listening.
attaches: Verb stem + -면서 after a vowel or ㄹ, -으면서 after a consonant (먹으면서). ㄷ-irregular verbs change: 듣다 → 들으면서.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
We talked while drinking coffee.

note: The subject of both clauses must be the same.

title: or
explain: Use -거나 to give a choice between actions: 보거나 만나요 = watch or meet.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -거나, the same after a vowel or a consonant.

examples.en: On weekends I watch a movie or meet a friend.
When I'm tired, I rest or sleep.

note: It joins clauses (verbs); to say 'or' between nouns use N(이)나.

title: while, during
explain: Use -는 동안 for what happens during a period when someone else does something: 요리하는 동안 = while cooking.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 동안, after a vowel or a consonant; ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 사는 동안).

examples.en: While I cooked, my younger sibling cleaned.

examples.ko: 한국에 사는 동안 많은 친구를 사귀었어요.
examples.en: While living in Korea, I made many friends.
examples.rom: hanguge saneun dongan maneun chingureul sagwieosseoyo

note: The subjects of the two clauses can differ, unlike -(으)면서.

title: it's been … since
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ 지 N이/가 되다 to say how long it has been since something happened: 온 지 일 년 = a year since I came.
attaches: Verb stem + -은 지 after a consonant, -ㄴ 지 after a vowel, followed by a time expression + 이/가 되다. ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 산 지).

examples.ko: 한국에 온 지 일 년이 됐어요.
examples.en: It has been a year since I came to Korea.
examples.rom: hanguge on ji il nyeoni dwaesseoyo

examples.ko: 한국어를 공부한 지 삼 개월이 됐어요.
examples.en: It has been three months since I started studying Korean.
examples.rom: hangugeoreul gongbuhan ji sam gaewori dwaesseoyo

note: 지 is written with a space before it. The verb is always in the past form -(으)ㄴ, even though the sentence describes elapsed time.

title: both…and, sometimes…sometimes
explain: Use -기도 하고 -기도 하다 to list two things you do: 보기도 하고 하기도 해요 = sometimes watch, sometimes do.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -기도 하고, repeated with a second stem + -기도 하다, with no change after a vowel or a consonant.

examples.ko: 주말에는 영화를 보기도 하고 운동을 하기도 해요.
examples.en: On weekends I sometimes watch movies and sometimes exercise.
examples.rom: jumareneun yeonghwareul bogido hago undongeul hagido haeyo

examples.ko: 그 식당은 맛있기도 하고 싸기도 해요.
examples.en: That restaurant is both tasty and cheap.
examples.rom: geu sikdangeun masitgido hago ssagido haeyo

note: Both parts should use the same form, and 하다 at the end takes the tense.

title: on the way
explain: Use -는 길에 to say what you do while heading somewhere: 오는 길에 = on the way here.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 길에, mostly with movement verbs such as 가다 and 오다. ㄹ-stem verbs drop ㄹ (살다 → 사는).

examples.en: I bought bread on the way home.
I mailed a letter on my way to school.

note: It describes doing something else while traveling, so the verb before it is normally a movement verb.

meaning: while doing, switch to another action
title: while doing, then switch
explain: Use -다가 when you were doing something and it got interrupted or changed: 가다가 = while going, then...
attaches: Verb stem + -다가, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (가다 → 가다가, 먹다 → 먹다가).

examples.en: I ran into a friend while I was going to school.
I was watching TV and fell asleep.

note: The first action is interrupted rather than completed, and the subject is usually the same in both clauses.

title: as soon as
explain: Use -자마자 when the next thing happens right away: 도착하자마자 = as soon as I arrive.
attaches: Verb stem + -자마자, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (오다 → 오자마자, 먹다 → 먹자마자).

examples.en: I took a shower as soon as I got home.
I met my friend as soon as class ended.

note: Do not put a tense marker (-았/었-) before -자마자; the tense goes on the final verb.

title: while staying that way
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ 채(로) to say you did something while leaving something in the same state: 불을 켠 채로 = with the light left on.
attaches: Verb stem + -은 채(로) after a consonant, -ㄴ 채(로) after a vowel, with the verb in the past form (켜다 → 켠 채).

examples.en: I fell asleep with the light on.
I went into the room with my shoes on.

note: It is used with verbs whose result state continues; it is not used for two actions happening at the same time.

title: to do both… and…
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 겸 to say you do something for two purposes at once: 운동도 할 겸 = to get some exercise too.
attaches: Verb stem + -을 겸 after a consonant, -ㄹ 겸 after a vowel. It is often paired as -(으)ㄹ 겸 -(으)ㄹ 겸, or used as N 겸 N.

examples.en: I walked there to get some exercise too.
I went to the park partly to get some fresh air.

note: It states more than one purpose for an action, and the main clause usually has a movement or action verb.

title: not only… but also
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 to add a second good point on top of the first: 맛있을 뿐만 아니라 = not only tasty.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 뿐만 아니라 after a consonant, -ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 after a vowel. With nouns, use N뿐만 아니라 or N일 뿐만 아니라.

examples.ko: 이 식당은 음식이 맛있을 뿐만 아니라 값도 싸요.
examples.en: This restaurant's food is not only tasty but also cheap.
examples.rom: i sikdangeun eumsigi masisseul ppunman anira gapdo ssayo

examples.ko: 그 친구는 노래를 잘할 뿐만 아니라 춤도 잘 춰요.
examples.en: That friend not only sings well but also dances well.
examples.rom: geu chinguneun noraereul jalhal ppunman anira chumdo jal chwoyo

note: The second clause adds a similar point and usually takes 도.

meaning: while at it; taking the opportunity
title: while you're at it
explain: Use -는 김에 to say you did one more thing since you were already doing something else: 가는 김에 = since I'm going anyway.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 김에, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ: 만들다 → 만드는 김에).

examples.ko: 시장에 가는 김에 과일도 사 왔어요.
examples.en: Since I was going to the market anyway, I bought some fruit too.
examples.rom: sijange ganeun gime gwaildo sa wasseoyo

examples.en: While I was cleaning anyway, I washed the windows too.

note: The second action is an extra, convenient one done during the same occasion as the first.

title: while someone is busy
explain: Use -는 사이에 to say something happened during the time another action was going on: 요리하는 사이에 = while cooking.
attaches: Action verb stem + -는 사이에, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (요리하는 사이에, 먹는 사이에). ㄹ-stem verbs drop ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 사이에).

examples.ko: 엄마가 요리하는 사이에 아이가 숙제를 끝냈어요.
examples.en: While Mom was cooking, the child finished his homework.
examples.rom: eommaga yorihaneun saie aiga sukjereul kkeunnaesseoyo

examples.en: It rained while I was asleep.

note: It stresses something happening in a short gap while the other action goes on, often unnoticed by the subject.

title: because, since
explain: Give a reason and then ask or suggest something: 바쁘니까 전화해 주세요 = I'm busy, so please call.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -으니까 after a consonant (먹으니까), -니까 after a vowel (가니까). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살다 → 사니까), and ㅂ-irregular stems become 우 (춥다 → 추우니까).

examples.en: I'm busy now, so please call me later.
It's cold, so dress warmly.

note: Unlike -아서/어서, it can be followed by commands and suggestions.

title: because, so
explain: Add -아서/어서 to an action or description to give a reason: 비가 와서 = because it rained.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -아서 after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (와서), -어서 after other vowels (먹어서), and 하다 becomes 해서.

examples.en: Because it rained, I stayed home.
I was so tired that I went to bed early.

note: It cannot be used with -았/었- before it, and the second clause cannot be a command or a suggestion.

title: because (of the fact)
explain: Use -기 때문에 to state a reason in a clear, slightly firm way: 비가 오기 때문에 = because it is raining.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -기 때문에, with no change after a vowel or a consonant. After a noun use N 때문에, or N(이)기 때문에.

examples.en: We canceled the picnic because it is raining.

examples.ko: 길이 막히기 때문에 저는 지하철을 타요.
examples.en: Because the roads get jammed, I take the subway.
examples.rom: giri makigi ttaemune jeoneun jihacheoreul tayo

note: It states the reason firmly, and commands and suggestions are not natural in the second clause.

title: because it is…
explain: Add N(이)라서 after a noun to say because it is that thing: 휴일이라서 = because it's a holiday.
attaches: Noun + 이라서 after a consonant (학생이라서), 라서 after a vowel (의사라서).

examples.en: Because today is a holiday, there are many people.
Because I'm a foreigner, Korean is hard for me.

note: It is the -아서/어서 form of 이다, so it also cannot take commands or suggestions.

title: thanks to
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 덕분에 to give credit for a good result: 도와주신 덕분에 = thanks to your help.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 덕분에 (present), or -(으)ㄴ 덕분에 (past: 도와주신 덕분에). Adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 덕분에 (좋은 덕분에). Noun + 덕분에.

examples.en: Thanks to the teacher's help, I passed the exam.
Thanks to the good weather, the trip was enjoyable.

note: It is only for positive results, and for negative results use -(으)ㄴ/는 탓에 or -는 바람에.

title: afraid that, in case
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ까 봐 to say you did something because you worried about what might happen: 늦을까 봐 = afraid I'd be late.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을까 봐 after a consonant (많을까 봐), -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel (올까 봐).

examples.en: I took a taxi because I was afraid I'd be late.
I brought an umbrella in case it rains.

note: It expresses worry about a possible future event, and the second clause is the action taken because of that worry.

title: you see, because
explain: Add -거든요 to give a reason or background the other person may not know: 바쁘거든요 = you see, I'm busy.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -거든요 with no change for vowels or consonants. Past is -았/었거든요, and with nouns use N이거든요.

examples.en: I can't go today. You see, I have a lot of work.
I've already seen that movie, you see.

note: It gives a reason or background that the listener does not know; it is not used for information the listener already shares (use -잖아요).

meaning: because of doing (busy with), often negative result
title: because I was busy doing
explain: Use -느라고 to say you were busy doing one thing, so something else didn't work out: 공부하느라고 = busy studying.
attaches: Action verb stem + -느라고, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (하느라고, 먹느라고). ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ out (놀다 → 노느라고).

examples.en: I couldn't sleep because I was busy studying for the exam.
I couldn't meet my friend because I was busy with my part-time job.

note: It needs the same subject in both clauses and an action verb, and it cannot be used with commands or suggestions.

title: because of
explain: Add N때문에 after a word to give the reason, often a bad result: 비 때문에 = because of the rain.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (비 때문에, 감기 때문에).

examples.en: We couldn't go on the picnic because of the rain.
I didn't come to school because of a cold.

note: It is often used for negative causes; it cannot be used with a command or suggestion in the second clause naturally.

meaning: as a result of too much
title: so much that
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ 나머지 to say that doing something too much led to a bad result: 긴장한 나머지 = so nervous that...
attaches: Verb stem + -(으)ㄴ 나머지, as -ㄴ after a vowel (놀란 나머지) and -은 after a consonant (먹은 나머지). Adjectives can also take it (피곤한 나머지).

examples.ko: 너무 긴장한 나머지 말이 안 나왔어요.
examples.en: I was so nervous that I couldn't speak.
examples.rom: neomu ginjanghan nameoji mari an nawasseoyo

examples.ko: 일에 열중한 나머지 밥 먹는 것을 잊었어요.
examples.en: I was so absorbed in work that I forgot to eat.
examples.rom: ire yeoljunghan nameoji bap meongneun geoseul ijeosseoyo

note: It states an excessive degree as the cause of an unintended or negative result; it can't be used for commands or suggestions.

title: as much as, since
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 만큼 to say the result matches the amount of something, or give a reason: 노력한 만큼 = as much as you tried.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 만큼 in the present; past -(으)ㄴ 만큼 (after a consonant -은, after a vowel -ㄴ); future -(으)ㄹ 만큼. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 만큼.

examples.en: You get results as much as you put in effort.

examples.ko: 아이가 있는 만큼 조심해서 운전해야 해요.
examples.en: Since I have a child, I have to drive carefully.
examples.rom: aiga inneun mankeum josimhaeseo unjeonhaeya haeyo

note: It has two meanings, 'to the same degree as' and 'since', so context decides; don't confuse it with the noun N만큼.

title: because of (blaming)
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 탓에 to blame a bad result on something: 추운 탓에 = because of the cold.
attaches: Adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 탓에 (추운 탓에), verb stem + -는 탓에 (present) or -(으)ㄴ 탓에 (past: 일어난 탓에). Noun + 탓에, or N인 탓에.

examples.en: Because of the cold weather, I caught a cold.
Because I got up late, I missed the bus.

note: It assigns blame for a bad result, so it is not used for good outcomes.

title: therefore (formal)
explain: Use -(으)므로 in formal writing or speeches to give a reason: 비가 많이 오므로 = since it rains a lot.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -으므로 after a consonant (많으므로), -므로 after a vowel (오므로). Noun + (이)므로 (휴일이므로).

examples.ko: 이 지역은 비가 많이 오므로 홍수에 주의해야 해요.
examples.en: Since it rains a lot in this area, you must watch out for floods.
examples.rom: i jiyeogeun biga mani omeuro hongsue juuihaeya haeyo

examples.en: Since tomorrow is a holiday, the school is closed.

note: It is formal and used mostly in writing, announcements, and speeches, so it sounds stiff in casual conversation.

title: seeing that, so
explain: Use -기에 to say you did something because of what you noticed: 날씨가 좋기에 = seeing the weather was nice.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -기에, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (좋기에, 싸기에).

examples.en: The weather was nice, so I went out for a walk.
The price was cheap, so I bought one.

note: The second clause is the speaker's action in response to what was seen or judged, and it is not used with commands.

meaning: because (I saw that) … so I did
title: since I saw that
explain: Use -길래 to say you did something because of what you saw or noticed: 울길래 = since (my friend) was crying.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -길래, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (울길래, 좋길래).

examples.en: My friend was crying, so I asked why.
There was a sale, so I bought clothes.

note: It is colloquial, and the second clause is usually a past action the speaker took in response to something observed. It is also used in questions like 뭐길래 (what is it that...).

meaning: as a result of (unexpected negative cause)
title: because of an unlucky event
explain: Use -는 바람에 to say something unexpected and bad happened and caused a problem: 막히는 바람에 = because of the traffic jam.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 바람에, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (막히는 바람에, 먹는 바람에). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (놀다 → 노는 바람에).

examples.en: Because of the traffic jam, I was late for my appointment.

examples.ko: 휴대폰이 고장 나는 바람에 연락을 못 했어요.
examples.en: My phone broke, so I couldn't get in touch.
examples.rom: hyudaeponi gojang naneun barame yeollageul mot haesseoyo

note: It is used only with verbs for an unexpected cause with a negative result, and it cannot take commands or suggestions.

title: when
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 때 to say at what time something happens: 시간이 있을 때 = when you have time.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -ㄹ 때 after a vowel, -을 때 after a consonant (먹을 때). ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (놀 때).

examples.en: Please call me when you have time.

examples.ko: 한국에 갈 때 비행기를 탈 거예요.
examples.en: I'll take a plane when I go to Korea.
examples.rom: hanguge gal ttae bihaenggireul tal geoyeyo

note: The tense of the main verb shows whether the time is past or future, and -았/었을 때 means 'when/after it happened'.

title: if, when
explain: Add -(으)면 to say what happens if or when something takes place: 비가 오면 = if it rains.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -으면 after a consonant (먹으면), -면 after a vowel (가면). 있다 becomes 있으면, and ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before ㅁ-type endings, so 살다 becomes 살면.

examples.en: If it rains, I will stay home.
If you have time, let's watch a movie together.

note: Don't put a past or future tense marker before -(으)면 in simple conditions; use the tense in the main clause.

title: every time
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 때마다 to say something always happens whenever another thing does: 들을 때마다 = every time I hear.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 때마다 after a consonant, -ㄹ 때마다 after a vowel (ㄹ-stems: 만들다 → 만들 때마다).

examples.ko: 이 노래를 들을 때마다 고향이 생각나요.
examples.en: Every time I hear this song, I think of my hometown.
examples.rom: i noraereul deureul ttaemada gohyangi saenggangnayo

examples.en: We have coffee every time I meet my friend.

note: N마다 attaches only to nouns. For verbs you need -(으)ㄹ 때마다.

title: if you want to
explain: Use -(으)려면 to say what is needed if you want to do something: 잘하려면 = if you want to be good at it.

sample.en: if you want to do well

attaches: Verb stem + -으려면 after a consonant (먹으려면), -려면 after a vowel (가려면). It is only used with action verbs, and ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (살려면).

examples.en: If you want to speak Korean well, you have to practice every day.
If you want to go to Seoul Station, take the subway.

note: The subject of both clauses must be the same, and the main clause usually has a command, suggestion or necessity.

meaning: only if; must in order to
title: only if, you must
explain: Use -아야/어야 to say something is needed before a result can happen: 공부해야 = only if you study.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -아야 after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (가야), -어야 after other vowels (먹어야), and 하다 becomes 해야. Irregular stems change as usual (듣다 becomes 들어야).

examples.en: Only if you study hard can you pass.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋아야 산에 갈 수 있어요.
examples.en: We can go to the mountain only if the weather is good.
examples.rom: nalssiga joaya sane gal su isseoyo

note: It expresses a necessary condition (only if), so it is not interchangeable with -(으)면, and the main clause is usually not a simple statement of fact that happens regardless.

title: now that
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 이상 to say that since something is already so, a result follows: 약속한 이상 = now that I've promised.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 이상 in the present, past -(으)ㄴ 이상; adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 이상. 이다 becomes 인 이상.

examples.ko: 약속을 한 이상 꼭 지켜야 해요.
examples.en: Now that you've made a promise, you must keep it.
examples.rom: yaksogeul han isang kkok jikyeoya haeyo

examples.ko: 학생인 이상 공부를 열심히 해야 해요.
examples.en: Since you are a student, you have to study hard.
examples.rom: haksaengin isang gongbureul yeolsimhi haeya haeyo

note: The main clause usually expresses obligation, determination or an inevitable conclusion, not a simple cause and effect.

title: as long as
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 한 to say something holds only while a condition lasts: 살아 있는 한 = as long as I'm alive.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 한 in the present; adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 한 (after a consonant -은, after a vowel -ㄴ). It is often used with 있다/없다 (있는 한, 없는 한).

examples.ko: 제가 살아 있는 한 당신을 지킬게요.
examples.en: As long as I'm alive, I will protect you.
examples.rom: jega sara inneun han dangsineul jikilgeyo

examples.ko: 비가 그치지 않는 한 출발할 수 없어요.
examples.en: We can't set off as long as the rain doesn't stop.
examples.rom: biga geuchiji anneun han chulbalhal su eopseoyo

note: It sets a limiting condition, so the main clause is usually something that can't hold when the condition breaks, and negative clauses are common.

title: in case of
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 경우에 to talk about what to do if something might happen: 비가 올 경우에 = in case it rains.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 경우에 after a consonant (없을 경우에), -ㄹ 경우에 after a vowel (갈 경우에). The 에 can be dropped.

examples.ko: 비가 올 경우에 행사는 실내에서 해요.
examples.en: In case it rains, the event is held indoors.
examples.rom: biga ol gyeongue haengsaneun sillaeeseo haeyo

examples.ko: 문제가 생길 경우에 이 번호로 전화하세요.
examples.en: In case a problem arises, call this number.
examples.rom: munjega saenggil gyeongue i beonhoro jeonhwahaseyo

note: It sounds formal and is common in notices and instructions; it names a possible situation rather than a worry.

title: if... then do
explain: Say 'if this happens' and then give a request or suggestion: 시간이 있거든 = if you have time (then come).
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -거든, with no change after vowels or consonants. The main clause is usually a command or suggestion.

examples.ko: 시간이 있거든 우리 집에 놀러 오세요.
examples.en: If you have time, come visit our house.
examples.rom: sigani itgeodeun uri jibe nolleo oseyo

examples.en: If there is a word you don't know, ask me.

note: Don't confuse it with sentence-ending -거든요 (giving a reason); this conditional -거든 is followed by a command or suggestion.

meaning: whenever; as long as one just
title: whenever I just
explain: Use -기만 하면 to say that one action always leads to another: 오기만 하면 = whenever (he) just comes.
attaches: Verb stem + -기만 하면, with no change after vowels or consonants. Adjectives can also be used (좋기만 하면).

examples.ko: 동생은 집에 오기만 하면 잠을 자요.
examples.en: My younger sibling sleeps whenever he just gets home.
examples.rom: dongsaengeun jibe ogiman hamyeon jameul jayo

examples.en: With this medicine, I get sleepy whenever I just take it.

note: The 만 emphasizes that this one action alone triggers the result, which is often unwanted or surprising.

meaning: if it is the case that
title: if it's the case that
explain: Use -다면 to say what you'll do if something turns out to be true: 비가 온다면 = if it rains.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -다면 (the plain form -다 plus -면). Past -았/었다면, and nouns take -(이)라면.

examples.en: If it rains tomorrow, I'll cancel the appointment.

examples.ko: 돈이 많다면 세계 여행을 하고 싶어요.
examples.en: If I had a lot of money, I would want to travel the world.
examples.rom: doni mantamyeon segye yeohaengeul hago sipeoyo

note: It treats the condition as an assumption or hypothetical, so it often sounds more tentative than -(으)면.

title: if only I had
explain: Use -았/었더라면 to wish the past had gone differently, saying what would have happened: 공부했더라면 = if only I had studied.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -았더라면 after ㅏ/ㅗ (갔더라면), -었더라면 after other vowels (먹었더라면), and 하다 becomes 했더라면.

examples.en: If I had studied hard then, I would have passed.
If we had left early, we wouldn't have been late.

note: It describes an unreal past condition and the main clause usually expresses regret or a different outcome, such as -았/었을 텐데.

title: but, although
explain: Join two ideas that contrast: 맵지만 맛있어요 = it's spicy, but tasty.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -지만, with no change after vowels or consonants. Past is -았/었지만.

examples.en: This food is spicy, but it's delicious.

examples.ko: 저는 한국어를 공부하지만 아직 잘 못해요.
examples.en: I study Korean, but I'm not good at it yet.
examples.rom: jeoneun hangugeoreul gongbuhajiman ajik jal mothaeyo

note: Don't attach it to a noun directly; use N이지만 (e.g., 학생이지만).

title: and, but (background)
explain: Set the scene or add a gentle contrast before your main point: 비가 오는데 = it's raining, and...
attaches: Verb stem + -는데 in the present; adjectives and 이다 take -(으)ㄴ데 (after a consonant -은데, after a vowel -ㄴ데). 있다/없다 take -는데, and past is -았/었는데.

examples.en: It's raining, and I don't have an umbrella.
This outfit is pretty, but it's too expensive.

note: It often sets up background for what follows, and the contrast is softer than -지만.

title: even if
explain: Use -아도/어도 to say something holds despite a condition: 비가 와도 = even if it rains.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -아도 after the vowels ㅏ/ㅗ (가도), -어도 after other vowels (먹어도), and 해도 for 하다 verbs.

examples.en: I will go even if it rains.
Even though I am tired, I exercise every day.

note: It is also the base of -아도/어도 되다 (may), which has a different meaning.

title: not A but B
explain: Use N이/가 아니라 N to correct something by saying what it is not, then what it is: 소금이 아니라 설탕 = not salt but sugar.
attaches: Noun + 이 아니라 after a consonant (소금이 아니라), 가 아니라 after a vowel (친구가 아니라). It negates the first noun and gives the correct one.

examples.en: This is not salt but sugar.
I am not a student but a teacher.

note: For verbs and adjectives, use -지 않고 or -(이)가 아니라 with a noun clause instead; this form only negates nouns.

title: whereas
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 반면(에) to set a good point against a bad point of the same thing: 싼 반면에 = cheap, whereas...
attaches: Verb + -는 반면에, adjective + -ㄴ 반면에 after a vowel or -은 반면에 after a consonant, past -았/었던 반면에, and noun + 인 반면에.

examples.ko: 이 집은 값이 싼 반면에 교통이 불편해요.
examples.en: This house is cheap, but on the other hand the transportation is inconvenient.
examples.rom: i jibeun gapsi ssan banmyeone gyotongi bulpyeonhaeyo

examples.en: My younger sibling is lively, whereas I am quiet.

note: It contrasts two opposite facts or characteristics, so the two clauses must be genuinely opposed.

title: even though (it happened)
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는데도 when a real fact led to a surprising result: 공부했는데도 = even though I studied.
attaches: Verb present -는데도, adjective -ㄴ데도 after a vowel or -은데도 after a consonant, past -았/었는데도, and noun + 인데도.

examples.en: Even though I studied hard, I failed the exam.
Even though the weather is cold, many people came out.

note: It states an actual fact with an unexpected result, unlike -아도/어도, which can be hypothetical.

title: yet also
explain: Use -(으)면서도 to say something has two qualities that seem opposite: 가เบา우면서도 튼튼해요 = light yet sturdy.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -으면서도 after a consonant, -면서도 after a vowel. Noun + 이면서도.

examples.en: This bag is light and yet sturdy.
He pretends not to know even though he knows.

note: Both clauses need the same subject; it is not just simultaneous action like -(으)면서.

title: although (hoped otherwise)
explain: Use -건만 to say that despite effort or expectation, the result disappointed: 노력했건만 = although I tried.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -건만, including past -았/었건만. It is mostly literary or formal.

examples.en: Although I tried hard, the result was not good.

examples.ko: 날씨가 이렇게 춥건만 그는 반팔을 입고 있어요.
examples.en: Although the weather is this cold, he is wearing short sleeves.
examples.rom: nalssiga ireoke chupgeonman geuneun banpareul ipgo isseoyo

note: It implies disappointment or surprise that an expected result did not occur, and is rare in casual speech.

title: true, but...
explain: Admit something is true, then add a 'but': 예쁘기는 하지만 = it is pretty, but...
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -기는 하지만, regardless of final consonant. It concedes the first clause before giving a contrasting second clause.

examples.ko: 이 옷이 예쁘기는 하지만 너무 비싸요.
examples.en: It is true that this outfit is pretty, but it is too expensive.
examples.rom: i osi yeppeugineun hajiman neomu bissayo

examples.en: Korean is difficult, it's true, but it is fun.

note: For 하다 verbs, repeat the verb: 공부하기는 하지만. Do not shorten it incorrectly.

meaning: instead of doing; in return for
title: instead of doing
explain: Use -는 대신에 to say you do one thing in place of or in return for another: 쉬는 대신에 = instead of resting.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 대신에 (쉬는 대신에); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 대신에. After a noun, use N 대신에.

examples.en: I rest today and work tomorrow instead.

examples.ko: 주말에 일하는 대신에 평일에 하루 쉬어요.
examples.en: I work on the weekend, so in return I take a weekday off.
examples.rom: jumare ilhaneun daesine pyeongire haru swieoyo

note: It can mean either 'instead of' or 'in exchange for', so the second clause often compensates for the first.

meaning: past observation followed by contrasting/resulting event
title: it was..., but then
explain: Use -더니 to say what you saw before, followed by a change or result: 맑더니 = it was sunny, but then...
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -더니, with no change for final consonants. The speaker has directly observed the first part.

examples.en: It was sunny in the morning, but it rains in the afternoon.

examples.ko: 동생이 어제는 열심히 공부하더니 오늘은 놀고 있어요.
examples.en: My sibling studied hard yesterday but is playing today.
examples.rom: dongsaengi eojeneun yeolsimhi gongbuhadeoni oneureun nolgo isseoyo

note: The subject is normally the third person (or second); the speaker must have witnessed the past situation.

title: more, the most
explain: Put 더/가장 before a describing word to say more or most: 더 좋아요 = I like it more.
attaches: These adverbs go directly before a verb or adjective and do not change form.

examples.en: I like autumn more than summer.

examples.ko: 저는 한국 음식 중에서 불고기를 가장 좋아해요.
examples.en: Among Korean foods, I like bulgogi the most.
examples.rom: jeoneun hanguk eumsik jungeseo bulgogireul gajang joahaeyo

note: 더 compares two things, while 가장 picks the top among three or more; 가장 is somewhat more formal than 제일.

title: become something
explain: Add N이/가 되다 after a thing or job to say what someone turns into: 의사가 되다 = become a doctor.

sample.en: I want to become a doctor

attaches: Noun + 이 되다 after a consonant (학생이 되다), + 가 되다 after a vowel (의사가 되다).

examples.en: I want to become a doctor.
My younger sibling became a university student.

note: The noun that you become takes 이/가, not 을/를.

title: the most
explain: Use N이/가 제일 A to say something is the best or most of all: 민수가 제일 키가 커요 = Minsu is the tallest.
attaches: Noun + 이 after a consonant or 가 after a vowel, then 제일 + adjective (or verb).

examples.ko: 제 친구 중에서 민수가 제일 키가 커요.
examples.en: Among my friends, Minsu is the tallest.
examples.rom: je chingu jungeseo minsuga jeil kiga keoyo

examples.ko: 이 가게에서는 이 빵이 제일 맛있어요.
examples.en: At this shop, this bread is the most delicious.
examples.rom: i gageeseoneun i ppangi jeil masisseoyo

note: The group is often marked with 중에서 or 에서; 제일 is more colloquial than 가장.
