title: more than
explain: Put N이/가 N보다 더 A between two things to say one is more than the other: 저 가방보다 더 비싸요 = more expensive than that bag.
attaches: First noun + 이 after a consonant or 가 after a vowel, second noun + 보다, then 더 + adjective (or verb).

examples.ko: 이 가방이 저 가방보다 더 비싸요.
examples.en: This bag is more expensive than that bag.
examples.rom: i gabangi jeo gabangboda deo bissayo

examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.

note: 더 can be omitted, but it makes the comparison clearer; the thing being compared to takes 보다, not 이/가.

title: describing a thing (adjective, past)
explain: Put -(으)ㄴ N before a noun to describe it with a quality or a past action: 예쁜 꽃 = pretty flower.
attaches: Adjective stem + -ㄴ after a vowel (예쁜 꽃) or -은 after a consonant (작은 집); past of verbs: stem + -ㄴ/은 (먹은 음식, 간 곳). ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (먼, 만든).

examples.en: I bought pretty flowers.
The food I ate yesterday was delicious.

note: With verbs this means completed action; with adjectives it is simply present description. 있다/없다 adjectives use -는 (맛있는).

title: become, get
explain: Add -아지다/어지다 to a describing word to say something changes into a new state: 따뜻해졌어요 = it got warm.
attaches: Adjective stem + -아지다 after ㅏ/ㅗ (좋아지다), -어지다 otherwise (커지다); 하다 becomes 해지다 (조용해지다).

examples.en: Since spring came, the weather has gotten warm.
My Korean skills have gotten much better.

note: Used with adjectives; with verbs it means a passive-like 'be done' (만들어지다).

title: more than
explain: Add N보다 after the thing you compare to: 어제보다 = than yesterday.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (나보다, 동생보다). The noun is the standard of comparison, and it is often used with 더.

examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.
My younger sibling is taller than me.

note: The noun marked with 보다 is the one being compared against, not the one that is bigger or more; word order is 'A는 B보다 ...'.

title: same as, different from
explain: Use N하고 같다/다르다 to compare two things as the same or different: 친구 가방하고 같아요 = same as my friend's bag.
attaches: Noun + 하고 before 같다 or 다르다; the noun ends in a vowel or consonant without any change.

examples.en: My bag is the same as my friend's bag.
Korean culture is different from my country's culture.

note: 하고 can be replaced by 와/과 (more formal) or (이)랑 (more casual); 다르다 is irregular (다르다 → 달라요).

title: rather than doing
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 것보다 to compare two actions or states: 쉬는 것보다 운동하는 게 좋아요 = exercising beats resting.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 것보다 (가는 것보다); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 것보다 (큰 것보다, 좋은 것보다). Past: -(으)ㄴ 것보다.

examples.ko: 집에서 쉬는 것보다 운동하는 게 좋아요.
examples.en: Exercising is better than resting at home.
examples.rom: jibeseo swineun geotboda undonghaneun ge joayo

examples.en: The test was harder than I thought.

note: It compares two actions or states; the second clause usually states the preferred one.

title: tend to, rather
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 편이다 to say what you are usually like or fairly like: 일찍 먹는 편이에요 = I tend to eat early.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 편이다 (먹는 편이다); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 편이다 after a consonant (작은 편이다), -ㄴ after a vowel (큰 편이다).

examples.en: I tend to eat breakfast early.
The prices at this restaurant are rather cheap.

note: It describes a general tendency, not an exact fact, so it is softer than a plain statement.

title: end up; come to
explain: Use -게 되다 when a situation develops on its own, not by your choice: 가게 되다 = it turns out I go.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -게 되다 (가게 되다, 알게 되다), with no change after a vowel or a consonant.

examples.en: It turned out that I'm going to Korea this year.

examples.ko: 한국 친구를 만나서 한국어를 좋아하게 됐어요.
examples.en: I met a Korean friend and came to like Korean.
examples.rom: hanguk chingureul mannaseo hangugeoreul joahage dwaesseoyo

note: It expresses a result due to circumstances, not your own decision (compare -기로 하다).

meaning: a noun that used to be/do
title: used to do
explain: Put -던 N before a noun to say something you used to do or go to: 가던 식당 = restaurant I used to go to.

sample.en: restaurant I used to go to

attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -던 + noun, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (가던 길, 먹던 빵). It recalls an action that was habitual or left unfinished.

examples.ko: 제가 자주 가던 식당이 문을 닫았어요.
examples.en: The restaurant I used to go to often has closed.
examples.rom: jega jaju gadeon sikdangi muneul dadasseoyo

examples.ko: 어릴 때 살던 집에 가 봤어요.
examples.en: I went to see the house where I lived as a child.
examples.rom: eoril ttae saldeon jibe ga bwasseoyo

note: -던 suggests repeated or interrupted action; -았/었던 suggests a completed past event.

title: end up; finish off
explain: Add -아/어 버리다 to an action to say you did it completely or with some regret: 먹어 버리다 = eat it all up.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 버리다 after ㅏ/ㅗ (가 버리다), -어 버리다 otherwise (먹어 버리다); 하다 becomes 해 버리다.

examples.ko: 배가 고파서 케이크를 다 먹어 버렸어요.
examples.en: I was hungry, so I ate the whole cake.
examples.rom: baega gopaseo keikeureul da meogeo beoryeosseoyo

examples.en: My friend has already gone off.

note: It can show relief or regret, depending on context.

title: feel, show feeling
explain: Use -아/어하다 to say what another person feels, not you: 무서워하다 = be afraid, show fear.
attaches: Adjective stem + -아하다 after ㅏ/ㅗ (좋아하다), -어하다 otherwise (무서워하다); 하다 becomes 해하다.

examples.en: My younger sibling is afraid of bugs.
The children like snow.

note: Used for a third person's feelings; the object takes 을/를 (벌레를 무서워해요), not 이/가.

title: as much as
explain: Add N만큼 after a word to say something is equal in amount or degree: 형만큼 = as much as my older brother.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (나만큼, 서울만큼). It expresses a similar degree or amount.

examples.en: I am as tall as my older brother too.
He sings as well as a singer.

note: It often pairs with a negative to mean 'not as ... as' (나는 형만큼 크지 않아요).

meaning: tend to be more … than N
title: tend to, more than
explain: Use N보다 -는 편이다 to say you usually do something more than someone else: 동생보다 많이 먹는 편이에요 = I tend to eat more.

sample.en: I tend to eat a lot

attaches: Noun + 보다, then a verb stem + -는 편이다 (먹는 편이에요); for adjectives use -(으)ㄴ 편이다 (큰 편이에요).

examples.en: I tend to eat more than my younger sibling.

examples.ko: 이 집은 다른 집보다 조용한 편이에요.
examples.en: This house is on the quiet side compared to other houses.
examples.rom: i jibeun dareun jipboda joyonghan pyeonieyo

note: 편이다 expresses a tendency, not an absolute statement.

title: like
explain: Add N처럼 after a word to say something is done or looks like that thing: 어른처럼 = like an adult.
attaches: Attaches directly to a noun, after a vowel or a consonant (새처럼, 친구처럼). It compares an action or state to the noun.

examples.en: That child talks like an adult.
We get along like family.

note: It is nearly interchangeable with N같이, but 처럼 is more common in speech.

title: compared to
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 데 비해(서) to compare one thing against how another thing is: 맛있는 데 비해서 = compared to how tasty it is.
attaches: Verb + -는 데 비해서, adjective + -ㄴ 데 비해서 after a vowel or -은 데 비해서 after a consonant. Past is -았/었던 데 비해서.

examples.ko: 이 식당은 음식이 맛있는 데 비해서 가격이 싸요.
examples.en: Compared to how delicious the food is, this restaurant is cheap.
examples.rom: i sikdangeun eumsigi masinneun de bihaeseo gagyeogi ssayo

examples.ko: 월급이 많은 데 비해서 저축은 적어요.
examples.en: Compared to the high salary, my savings are small.
examples.rom: wolgeubi maneun de bihaeseo jeochugeun jeogeoyo

note: With a plain noun, use N에 비해(서) instead.

meaning: amounts to; is as good as
title: as good as; amounts to
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 to say something is basically the same as something else: 매일 만나는 셈이다 = it's as good as meeting daily.
attaches: Verb stem + -는 셈이다 (present); past -(으)ㄴ 셈이다 (먹은 셈이다, 간 셈이다); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 셈이다; ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (사는 셈이다).

examples.ko: 일주일에 다섯 번 만나니까 매일 만나는 셈이에요.
examples.en: We meet five times a week, so it amounts to meeting every day.
examples.rom: iljuire daseot beon mannanikka maeil mannaneun semieyo

examples.ko: 숙제를 거의 다 했으니까 끝낸 셈이에요.
examples.en: I've done almost all of the homework, so it's as good as finished.
examples.rom: sukjereul geoui da haesseunikka kkeunnaen semieyo

note: Do not confuse it with -(으)ㄹ 셈이다, which means 'intend to'; -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 expresses a conclusion or evaluation.

title: the more, the more
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ수록 to say that as one thing increases, so does another: 공부할수록 재미있어요 = the more I study, the more fun.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을수록 after a consonant (읽을수록), -ㄹ수록 after a vowel (갈수록). ㄹ-stems drop to -ㄹ수록 (살수록).

examples.en: The more I study Korean, the more fun it is.
The more I eat the food, the more I want to eat.

note: Often paired with 더 in the second clause; no tense marker goes before -(으)ㄹ수록.

title: I'd rather not
explain: Use -느니 to say you'd choose something else over a bad option: 가느니 안 가겠어요 = I'd rather not go.
attaches: Verb stem + -느니 directly (먹느니, 가느니); used only with verbs.

examples.en: I'd rather not go than go alone.

examples.ko: 그 사람에게 부탁하느니 내가 직접 할게요.
examples.en: Rather than ask that person, I'll do it myself.
examples.rom: geu saramege butakaneuni naega jikjeop halgeyo

note: Used only with verbs; the second clause often uses 차라리 (rather).

meaning: if you keep doing, you will find
title: if you keep doing
explain: Use -다가 보면 to say that if you keep at something, a result will come: 공부하다가 보면 = if you keep studying.
attaches: Verb stem + -다가 보면, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (하다가 보면, 먹다가 보면).

examples.ko: 한국어를 계속 공부하다가 보면 잘하게 될 거예요.
examples.en: If you keep studying Korean, you will become good at it.
examples.rom: hangugeoreul gyesok gongbuhadaga bomyeon jalhage doel geoyeyo

examples.en: If you keep exercising regularly, you become healthy.

note: It describes a result you discover after repeating an action; it is not used for a result that has already happened.

title: just as, as if
explain: Use -듯이 to say something happens just like or as if something else: 비가 오듯이 = as if it were raining.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -듯이 directly, with no consonant/vowel change (먹듯이, 가듯이). Past: -았/었듯이.

examples.en: Sweat poured down as if it were raining.

examples.ko: 아시다시피 알다시피 말하듯이 쉽게 설명해 주세요.
examples.en: Please explain it easily, as if you were just talking.
examples.rom: asidasipi aldasipi malhadeusi swipge seolmyeonghae juseyo

note: Often shortened to -듯; 듯이 compares manner, and differs from -는 듯하다 (it seems).

title: just the same as
explain: Add N(이)나 마찬가지다 after a word to say something is practically the same as another thing: 끝난 거나 마찬가지 = as good as finished.
attaches: Noun + 이나 마찬가지다 after a consonant (거지나 마찬가지예요 uses 나 after a vowel), 나 마찬가지다 after a vowel.

examples.en: That job is as good as finished.
These clothes are just the same as new ones.

note: It means practically the same as, not exactly identical.

title: not as good as
explain: Add N만 못하다 after something to say it falls short of it: 예전 맛만 못해요 = not as good as the old taste.
attaches: Noun + 만 못하다 (못해요), with no change after a vowel or a consonant.

examples.en: Coffee these days isn't as good as the old taste.
This restaurant isn't as good as that one.

note: The noun is the better one; 'A is N만 못하다' means N is better than A.

title: compared to
explain: Add N에 비해(서) after a word to compare something against another: 작년에 비해 = compared to last year.
attaches: Attaches to a noun with no change after a vowel or a consonant (작년에 비해). Before a noun it becomes N에 비한 N.

examples.ko: 작년에 비해 올해는 눈이 많이 왔어요.
examples.en: Compared to last year, it snowed a lot this year.
examples.rom: jangnyeone bihae olhaeneun nuni mani wasseoyo

examples.en: Seoul has higher prices compared to the countryside.

note: It states a comparison with a standard; unlike 보다, it is not used with 더 in the same way.

title: will / must be
explain: Use -겠- to state what you will do or to guess something: 먹겠어요 = I will eat.
attaches: Added directly to a verb or adjective stem, whether it ends in a vowel or a consonant (가겠어요, 먹겠어요).

examples.en: I will eat first.
It looks like it will rain tomorrow.

note: With 'I' it shows intention or willingness, and with other subjects it shows inference. It is also used in set phrases like 잘 먹겠습니다.

meaning: it seems it will; I think
title: I think it will
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 to say what you guess will happen soon: 비가 올 것 같아요 = it looks like it will rain.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 것 같다 after a consonant (먹을 것 같아요), -ㄹ 것 같다 after a vowel (갈 것 같아요).

examples.en: It seems it will rain tomorrow.

examples.ko: 이 음식은 너무 매울 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think this food will be too spicy.
examples.rom: i eumsigeun neomu maeul geot gatayo

note: It expresses a guess about the future or an unknown; ㄹ-stems keep ㄹ (살 것 같아요).

title: it seems that
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 to say how things seem right now or what you guess happened: 자는 것 같아요 = he seems to be sleeping.
attaches: Verb + -는 것 같다 (먹는 것 같아요); adjective + -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 (예쁜 것 같아요, 좋은 것 같아요); past with verbs -(으)ㄴ 것 같다 (간 것 같아요).

examples.ko: 민수 씨는 지금 자는 것 같아요.
examples.en: It seems that Minsu is sleeping now.
examples.rom: minsu ssineun jigeum janeun geot gatayo

examples.ko: 이 옷이 더 좋은 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think this outfit is better.
examples.rom: i osi deo joeun geot gatayo

note: It is also used to soften opinions; do not use it for facts you know for certain.

title: as if, like
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 것처럼 to compare an action to something that seems true: 아는 것처럼 말해요 = talks as if he knows.
attaches: Present verb stem + -는 것처럼; adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 것처럼; past + -(으)ㄴ 것처럼; noun + 인 것처럼.

examples.ko: 그는 모든 걸 아는 것처럼 말해요.
examples.en: He talks as if he knows everything.
examples.rom: geuneun modeun geol aneun geotcheoreom malhaeyo

examples.ko: 그는 한국 사람인 것처럼 한국어를 잘해요.
examples.en: He speaks Korean well, as if he were Korean.
examples.rom: geuneun hanguk saramin geotcheoreom hangugeoreul jalhaeyo

note: It compares to a situation or state, and it is not necessarily the speaker's own judgment.

title: pretend to
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다 to say someone acts as if something is true when it isn't: 자는 척했어요 = pretended to sleep.
attaches: Present verb stem + -는 척하다 (자는 척하다); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (괜찮은 척하다); past verb stem + -(으)ㄴ 척하다. ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ (아는 척하다).

examples.en: My younger sibling pretended to be asleep.
I pretended to be fine.

note: -(으)ㄴ/는 체하다 means the same thing.

title: apparently
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는가 보다 when you guess something from what you just saw or heard: 비가 오는가 봐요 = apparently it's raining.
attaches: Verb stem + -는가 보다 (먹는가 봐요); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (좋은가 봐요, 예쁜가 봐요); noun + 인가 보다 (학생인가 봐요).

examples.en: It seems to be raining outside, apparently.

examples.ko: 저 식당은 맛있는가 봐요. 사람이 많아요.
examples.en: That restaurant must be good, as there are many people.
examples.rom: jeo sikdangeun masinneunga bwayo sarami manayo

note: It is based on evidence you observe, and cannot be used for your own feelings or actions.

meaning: when I did X, I found that
title: when I did, I found
explain: Use -(으)니까 (발견) to say that after you did something, you discovered something: 집에 가니까 = when I got home, I found...
attaches: Verb stem + -으니까 after a consonant (먹으니까), -니까 after a vowel (가니까). The following clause states a discovery, usually in past tense.

examples.en: When I got home, a package had arrived.
When I opened the window, it was very quiet outside.

note: Second example is wrong form: ㄹ-verbs drop ㄹ, so it should be 여니까.

title: probably, so…
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 텐데 to say what is probably true, then add advice or contrast: 막힐 텐데 = it'll probably be jammed, so…
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을 텐데 after a consonant (먹을 텐데), -ㄹ 텐데 after a vowel (갈 텐데); noun + 일 텐데 (학생일 텐데).

examples.ko: 지금 가면 길이 막힐 텐데 조금 이따가 가요.
examples.en: The roads will probably be jammed if you go now, so go a bit later.
examples.rom: jigeum gamyeon giri makil tende jogeum ittaga gayo

examples.en: You must be tired, so please rest a bit.

note: It states a guess and then leads into a related statement, so a following clause is expected.

title: might
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다 to say something is possible but not certain: 막힐지도 몰라요 = it might get jammed.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을지도 모르다 after a consonant (먹을지도 몰라요), -ㄹ지도 모르다 after a vowel (갈지도 몰라요).

examples.en: The roads might be jammed.
He may have already left.

note: It expresses a weaker possibility than -(으)ㄹ 것 같다; it is often used to warn.

title: I see, wow
explain: Use -군요/는군요 to react to something you just realized or found out: 오는군요 = oh, it's coming (raining)!
attaches: Verb stem + -는군요 (먹는군요, 가는군요); adjective stem and 이다 + -군요 (예쁘군요, 학생이군요). Past is -았/었군요.

examples.en: Oh, I see it's raining.
Wow, the house is really big.

note: It expresses a new realization or discovery; it is a bit more exclamatory than -네요.

title: oh, it is!
explain: Use -네요 when you notice or discover something right now: 잘하시네요 = oh, you do it well!
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -네요 with no change for vowels or consonants; stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 사네요). Past is -았/었네요.

examples.en: Oh, you speak Korean well.
Oh, it's raining outside.

note: It expresses surprise at something the speaker has just noticed or experienced directly.

title: thought/didn't know that
explain: Use -는 줄 알다/모르다 to say what you thought or didn't know was true: 시험이 있는 줄 몰랐어요 = I didn't know there was a test.

sample.en: I didn't know he was going

attaches: Present verb stem + -는 줄 (오는 줄); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ 줄 (큰 줄); past verb + -(으)ㄴ 줄 (간 줄); noun + 인 줄 (의사인 줄).

examples.ko: 저는 오늘 시험이 있는 줄 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I didn't know there was an exam today.
examples.rom: jeoneun oneul siheomi inneun jul mollasseoyo

examples.en: I thought it was raining, but it wasn't.

note: Don't confuse it with -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다, which means knowing how to do something.

meaning: softened ending giving background or mild reaction
title: softening, background info
explain: Put -는데요/-(으)ㄴ데요 at the end of a sentence to give background or a gentle reaction, so you sound polite: 안 계시는데요 = they're not here, I'm afraid.
attaches: Same stems as -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 plus 요: verb -는데요 (가는데요), adjective -ㄴ데요/-은데요 (좋은데요), noun 인데요.

examples.en: The boss isn't here right now, I'm afraid.
This outfit is a bit small, though.

note: The sentence trails off and implies a request, refusal, or mild objection without stating it.

title: look, seem
explain: Use -아/어 보이다 to say how someone or something looks from the outside: 좋아 보여요 = you look good.
attaches: Mainly adjective stem + -아 보이다 after ㅏ/ㅗ (좋아 보여요), -어 보이다 after other vowels (맛있어 보여요); 하다 becomes 해 보이다 (행복해 보여요).

examples.en: You look like you're in a good mood today.
This cake looks really delicious.

note: It describes appearance and attaches to adjectives; do not confuse it with -아/어 보다 (try).

title: as you know
explain: Use -잖아요 to remind someone of something they already know: 말했잖아요 = I told you, remember?
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -잖아요 with no change for vowels or consonants. Past is -았/었잖아요, and with nouns use N이잖아요.

examples.en: I told you yesterday, remember?
It's Sunday today, you know.

note: It reminds the listener of something they already know and can sound like a rebuke, so be careful with superiors.

title: judging from seeing
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는 걸 보니(까) to say you guess something because of what you see: 우산을 든 걸 보니 = judging from him holding an umbrella.

sample.en: judging from the fact he's going

attaches: Verb stem + -는 걸 보니(까) (먹는 걸 보니); adjective stem + -ㄴ/은 걸 보니(까) (예쁜 걸 보니); past -은 걸 보니; noun + 인 걸 보니.

examples.ko: 우산을 들고 있는 걸 보니 비가 오나 봐요.
examples.en: Judging from the fact that he's carrying an umbrella, it must be raining.
examples.rom: usaneul deulgo inneun geol boni biga ona bwayo

examples.ko: 얼굴이 밝은 걸 보니 좋은 일이 있었나 봐요.
examples.en: Judging from your bright face, something good must have happened.
examples.rom: eolguri balgeun geol boni joeun iri isseonna bwayo

note: The clause after it is the speaker's inference, usually ending in 것 같다, -나 보다, or -(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다.

title: know whether or how
explain: Use -(으)ㄴ/는지 알다/모르다 to say you know or don't know where, how, or whether something is: 어디 있는지 알아요? = do you know where it is?

sample.en: do you know where it is?

attaches: Verb stem + -는지 (가는지); adjective stem + -(으)ㄴ지 (큰지, 좋은지); past -았/었는지; noun + 인지. Followed by 알다 or 모르다.

examples.en: Do you know where that restaurant is?

examples.ko: 그 사람이 왜 화가 났는지 모르겠어요.
examples.en: I don't know why that person got angry.
examples.rom: geu sarami wae hwaga nanneunji moreugesseoyo

note: Used with question words or 'whether' (V-는지 아닌지); do not confuse with -는 줄 알다 (believe that).

title: it's natural that
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ 법하다 to say something is likely or only natural given the reason: 합격할 법해요 = it's likely you'll pass.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -ㄹ 법하다 after a vowel (올 법하다), -을 법하다 after a consonant (먹을 법하다).

examples.en: Since you studied so hard, it's likely you'll pass.

examples.ko: 그런 말을 들으면 화가 날 법해요.
examples.en: It's natural to get angry if you hear such words.
examples.rom: geureon mareul deureumyeon hwaga nal beopaeyo

note: It means 'it would be natural/plausible', so it fits reasoning about what normally happens.

meaning: I should have; I wish I had
title: should have done
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다 to say you regret not doing something: 가져올걸 그랬어요 = I should have brought it.
attaches: Verb stem + -을걸 그랬다 after a consonant (먹을걸 그랬어요), -ㄹ걸 그랬다 after a vowel (갈걸 그랬어요).

examples.en: I should have brought an umbrella.
I wish I had gone to bed early yesterday.

note: It expresses regret about something not done; for regret about something done, use -지 말걸 그랬다.

title: probably
explain: Use -(으)ㄹ걸요 to say what you guess will probably happen or be true: 올걸요 = it'll probably come.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -을걸요 after a consonant (많을걸요), -ㄹ걸요 after a vowel (올걸요). It also attaches to the past stem (갔을걸요).

examples.en: I think it will probably rain tomorrow.
I think Minsu is probably at home now.

note: It expresses a casual guess, often a gentle contradiction of what the listener assumes. Do not confuse it with -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다, which expresses regret.

title: oh, I see!
explain: Add -는구나 to a word to say you just noticed something, in a casual way: 오는구나 = oh, it's coming!
attaches: Verb stem + -는구나 (가는구나, 먹는구나); adjective and 이다 stems + -구나 (크구나, 학생이구나); past -았/었구나. Casual (반말) only.

examples.en: Oh, it's snowing already.
Wow, you're really tall.

note: Use with friends or younger people; to elders or in polite speech use -군요/는군요.

title: I saw that…
explain: Use -더- to tell what you personally saw or felt before: 많더라고요 = there were so many (I noticed).

sample.en: there were so many, I saw

attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -더- followed by an ending (-더라고요, -던데요, -더니); it can follow -았/었- (먹었더라고요).

examples.ko: 어제 공원에 가니까 사람이 정말 많더라고요.
examples.en: When I went to the park yesterday, I saw there were really a lot of people.
examples.rom: eoje gongwone ganikka sarami jeongmal manteoragoyo

examples.en: The food at that restaurant was good, I found.

note: It reports what the speaker directly witnessed or experienced; it is normally not used for the speaker's own deliberate actions.

title: I found that
explain: Use -더라고요 to tell what you experienced or noticed yourself in the past: 맛있더라고요 = I found it tasty.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -더라고요, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (맛있더라고요, 하더라고요). The past form is -았/었더라고요.

examples.ko: 어제 간 식당은 음식이 정말 맛있더라고요.
examples.en: I found that the food at the restaurant I went to yesterday was really good.
examples.rom: eoje gan sikdangeun eumsigi jeongmal masitdeoragoyo

examples.en: I noticed that Minsu studies at the library every day.

note: It reports something the speaker directly saw or experienced. It is not used for things the speaker has not witnessed.

meaning: after I did X, I found Y
title: after doing, I found
explain: Use -았/었더니 to say you did something and then noticed a result: 먹었더니 = after I ate it (I found...).
attaches: Verb stem + -았더니 after ㅏ/ㅗ (갔더니), -었더니 after other vowels (먹었더니), -했더니 for 하다 verbs. The speaker's own past action leads to a discovery or result.

examples.en: After I took medicine, my headache is gone.

examples.ko: 어제 운동을 많이 했더니 오늘 너무 피곤해요.
examples.en: I exercised a lot yesterday, so I'm very tired today.
examples.rom: eoje undongeul mani haetdeoni oneul neomu pigonhaeyo

note: The subject of the first clause is normally 'I' (first person); for another person's behavior use -더니.

title: I should have…, but
explain: Use -았/었어야 했는데 to say you regret not doing something: 일찍 잤어야 했는데 = I should have slept early, but...
attaches: Verb stem + -았어야 했는데 after ㅏ/ㅗ (갔어야 했는데), -었어야 했는데 after other vowels (먹었어야 했는데), 했어야 했는데 for 하다 verbs.

examples.ko: 어제 일찍 잤어야 했는데 늦게 잤어요.
examples.en: I should have slept early yesterday, but I slept late.
examples.rom: eoje iljjik jasseoya haenneunde neutge jasseoyo

examples.en: I should have booked in advance, but I forgot.

note: Expresses regret about a past action not taken; -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다 is a more casual alternative.

title: told someone to
explain: Use -(으)라고 하다 to pass on an order or instruction: 먹으라고 했어요 = told me to take it.
attaches: Verb stem + -으라고 하다 after a consonant (먹으라고 해요), -라고 하다 after a vowel (가라고 해요); negative -지 말라고 하다.

examples.en: The doctor told me to take the medicine.
My mom tells me to go to sleep early.

note: Only verbs can be used; the negative is -지 말라고 하다, not -지 않으라고 하다.

title: asked whether or what
explain: Use -냐고 하다 to pass on a question someone asked: 어디에 가냐고 했어요 = asked where I'm going.
attaches: Verb or adjective stem + -냐고 하다 (가냐고 해요, 작냐고 해요); verbs may also take -느냐고; past -았/었냐고; noun + (이)냐고 하다.

examples.en: My friend asked me where I was going.
The teacher asked whether I had done my homework.

note: The quoted question is in plain form, so the ending -냐고 stays the same and the person and tense words must be adjusted to the reporting perspective.

title: says that
explain: Use -다고 하다 to pass on what someone said: 시험이 있다고 해요 = they say there is an exam.
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄴ/는다고 하다 (먹는다고 해요, 간다고 해요); adjective stem + -다고 하다 (크다고 해요); past -았/었다고 하다; noun + (이)라고 하다.

examples.en: My friend says that there is an exam tomorrow.
My younger sibling said that they exercise every day these days.

note: Verbs take -ㄴ/는다고 but adjectives and 있다/없다 take -다고 (있다고, 없다고 is correct but 있는다고 is not).

title: you say…?
explain: Use -다고요? to check or react to what you just heard, or to repeat what you said: 휴가라고요? = You say it's vacation?
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄴ/는다고요? (간다고요?, 먹는다고요?); adjective stem + -다고요? (좋다고요?); noun + (이)라고요?

examples.en: You say it's vacation from tomorrow? Really?
I'm saying I didn't go. I was at home.

note: With rising intonation it asks for confirmation of what you heard; with falling intonation it repeats what you said, and it is somewhat impolite to elders.

title: suggested we do
explain: Use -자고 하다 to pass on someone's suggestion: 영화를 보자고 했어요 = suggested we watch a movie.
attaches: Verb stem + -자고 하다, with no change after a vowel or a consonant (가자고 해요, 먹자고 해요).

examples.ko: 친구가 주말에 같이 영화를 보자고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend suggested that we watch a movie together this weekend.
examples.rom: chinguga jumare gachi yeonghwareul bojago haesseoyo

examples.en: My coworkers suggest that we have lunch together.

note: It attaches only to verbs, and the negative is -지 말자고 하다 (suggesting we not do something).

title: is called
explain: Add N(이)라고 하다 after a name to say what something is called: 김밥이라고 해요 = it's called gimbap.
attaches: Noun + 이라고 하다 after a consonant (책이라고 해요), 라고 하다 after a vowel (커피라고 해요).

examples.en: This food is called gimbap.
My name is Sujin.

note: It is also used for introducing names or titles, and in speech it often shortens to N(이)래요.

title: I said so!
explain: Use -(느)ㄴ다니까 to insist on what you already said, often when annoyed: 안 간다니까 = I said I'm not going!
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄴ/는다니까 (간다니까, 먹는다니까); adjective stem + -다니까 (좋다니까); past -았/었다니까; noun + (이)라니까.

examples.ko: 제가 안 간다니까 왜 자꾸 물어봐요?
examples.en: I said I'm not going, so why do you keep asking?
examples.rom: jega an gandanikka wae jakku mureobwayo

examples.ko: 이게 진짜 맛있다니까요. 한번 먹어 봐요.
examples.en: I'm telling you this is really tasty. Try it.
examples.rom: ige jinjja masitdanikkayo hanbeon meogeo bwayo

note: It is a contraction of -다고 하니까 and sounds insistent or irritated, so be careful with elders.

title: I said do it!
explain: Use -(으)라고요 to repeat a command because someone didn't listen: 일어나라고요 = I said get up!
attaches: Verb stem + -으라고요 after a consonant (먹으라고요), -라고요 after a vowel (가라고요). A ㄹ-stem simply adds -라고요 (놀라고요).

examples.en: I said get up quickly!
I'm telling you to do your homework first.

note: It repeats a command with some irritation. It can also be a surprised check: 'You're telling me to...?'

title: I heard…, so
explain: Use -다고 하던데 to share something you heard and then add advice or a follow-up: 춥다고 하던데 = I heard it's cold, so...
attaches: Quoted ending -ㄴ/는다고, -다고, or (이)라고 + 하던데; verb stem + -ㄴ/는다고 하던데 (간다고 하던데), adjective stem + -다고 하던데 (춥다고 하던데).

examples.ko: 내일은 날씨가 춥다고 하던데 따뜻하게 입으세요.
examples.en: I heard it will be cold tomorrow, so dress warmly.
examples.rom: naeireun nalssiga chupdago hadeonde ttatteuthage ibeuseyo

examples.ko: 그 식당이 맛있다고 하던데 한번 가 볼까요?
examples.en: I heard that restaurant is good; shall we try it?
examples.rom: geu sikdangi masitdago hadeonde hanbeon ga bolkkayo

note: Reports hearsay and leads into a related comment or question; the speaker did not directly experience it.

title: just because
explain: Use -다고 해서 to say something is not necessarily true only because of a reason: 비싸다고 해서 = just because it's pricey.
attaches: Quoted-clause ending: verb stem + -ㄴ/는다고 해서 (간다고 해서, 먹는다고 해서), adjective stem + -다고 해서 (비싸다고 해서), noun + (이)라고 해서 (학생이라고 해서). Past: -았/었다고 해서.

examples.ko: 비싸다고 해서 다 좋은 건 아니에요.
examples.en: Just because something is expensive doesn't mean it's all good.
examples.rom: bissadago haeseo da joeun geon anieyo

examples.ko: 친구가 간다고 해서 저도 같이 갔어요.
examples.en: Because my friend said he was going, I went along too.
examples.rom: chinguga gandago haeseo jeodo gachi gasseoyo

note: Often paired with a negative ending (-는 건 아니다) to mean 'just because...'; it can also simply mean 'because someone said'.

title: the news that
explain: Use -다는 before a noun to say what the news, rumor or idea is: 비가 온다는 소식 = news that it'll rain.
attaches: Contracted from -다고 하는; verb stem + -ㄴ/는다는 (간다는), adjective stem + -다는 (좋다는), noun + (이)라는 (의사라는), then followed by a noun.

examples.en: I heard the news that it will rain tomorrow.
The saying that Korean food is spicy is true.

note: Used when the noun is content like 소식, 말, 생각, 이야기; do not use -는 N alone for such content clauses.

meaning: I heard that…, is that right?
title: I heard…, right?
explain: Use -다면서(요)? to check something you heard from someone: 이사한다면서요? = I heard you're moving, right?
attaches: Verb stem + -ㄴ/는다면서요? (간다면서요?); adjective stem + -다면서요? (좋다면서요?); past -았/었다면서요?; noun + (이)라면서요?

examples.en: I heard you're moving next week, is that right?
I heard that restaurant is very tasty, is that right?

note: It checks information the speaker has already heard; it is not for new questions.

meaning: ask someone to do for the speaker
title: asked me to do
explain: Use -아/어 달라고 하다 to say someone asked for a favor: 찍어 달라고 했어요 = asked me to take it for them.
attaches: Verb stem + -아 달라고 하다 after ㅏ/ㅗ (찾아 달라고 해요), -어 달라고 하다 otherwise (읽어 달라고 해요), 해 달라고 하다 for 하다.

examples.ko: 친구가 제게 사진을 찍어 달라고 했어요.
examples.en: My friend asked me to take a photo for them.
examples.rom: chinguga jege sajineul jjigeo dallago haesseoyo

examples.en: The child asks me to read a book to them.

note: Use it when the request benefits the speaker; if the request is for a third person, use -아/어 주라고 하다.
